title: Indiana Corn Farmers Applaud Use of Indiana Ethanol in INDYCAR Race Fuel
description:
The new fuel formulation will incorporate renewable ethanol sourced from Indiana, bringing together two of the state’s iconic industries – agriculture and motorsports.
The announcement also highlights the important role Indiana ethanol plays in creating markets for corn grown by Hoosier farmers.
“This is great news for Indiana farmers,” said J.R. Roesner, ICGA Board Member and corn farmer from Ferdinand, Ind.
For Indiana corn farmers, seeing their crop and its renewable products showcased in innovative competitions like motorsports is another example of the diverse markets created by Indiana’s corn industry.
Corn farmers who work within 30 miles of one of the state’s 15 ethanol plant can realize an 18-23 cent per bushel premium on corn prices.
text:
INDIANAPOLIS — The Indiana Corn Marketing Council (ICMC) and the Indiana Corn Growers Association (ICGA) are delighted to see Indiana-grown corn once again playing a role in the future of INDYCAR racing through Shell’s updated 100 percent Renewable Race Fuel, which will debut during the 2027 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season.

The new fuel formulation will incorporate renewable ethanol sourced from Indiana, bringing together two of the state’s iconic industries – agriculture and motorsports. The announcement also highlights the important role Indiana ethanol plays in creating markets for corn grown by Hoosier farmers.

“This is great news for Indiana farmers,” said J.R. Roesner, ICGA Board Member and corn farmer from Ferdinand, Ind. “Ethanol is a major industry in our state and accounts for more than 40 percent of our corn grind. It’s exciting to see a homegrown, renewable fuel from Indiana become part of the fuel powering INDYCAR race cars.”

On its website, INDYCAR reported the updated Shell 100 percent Renewable Race Fuel is expected to deliver at least a 70 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared with the Renewable Fuel Standard average gasoline baseline. The fuel will continue to meet the performance and durability requirements of INDYCAR and its engine manufacturers.

For Indiana corn farmers, seeing their crop and its renewable products showcased in innovative competitions like motorsports is another example of the diverse markets created by Indiana’s corn industry.

State Rep. J.D. Prescott (R-Union City), also an ICMC Board member, applauded Friday’s announcement. Nearly one year ago, Prescott called on INDYCAR to source its ethanol from Indiana, urging the racing series to support American farmers and domestic ethanol producers.

“Racing is a part of Indiana’s heritage, so it makes sense that the fuel powering these incredible race cars should support Hoosier farmers and workers,” Prescott said. “I’m proud to see INDYCAR make this change, bringing the purchase of ethanol back home. This decision will support Indiana’s corn farmers, strengthen our ethanol industry and benefit our state’s economy.”

This result could not have happened without the combined efforts of ICGA and ICMC. While ICGA campaigned state and federal lawmakers for more opportunities to expand Indiana’s ethanol industry, ICMC worked with ethanol producers to site new bioprocessing facilities throughout the state.

Indiana plants nearly 5.5 million acres of corn each year, and those acres yield more than 1 billion bushels. Indiana is the fifth-largest, corn-producing state in America. Corn farmers who work within 30 miles of one of the state’s 15 ethanol plant can realize an 18-23 cent per bushel premium on corn prices. At more than 1.4 billion gallons per year, Indiana is the fifth-largest U.S. producer of ethanol – accounting for nearly 8 percent of the total U.S. ethanol output.

“Since its creation in 2007, the Indiana Corn Marketing Council has worked diligently in making sure the infrastructure was in place so that Hoosier farmers could benefit from the opportunities of an expanding ethanol market,” said ICMC President Susan Brocksmith, a corn farmer from Vincennes, Ind. “This announcement is another success story from that work. Without the efforts of bringing 15 ethanol biorefineries into Indiana, we may not have had the ability to fulfill the needs to supply INDYCAR’s racing fuel needs.”

text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel Pioneer Completes Successful Trials

(Nova Pangea Technologies) Nova Pangaea Technologies, the UK company with a unique process to create sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from waste biomass, has completed successful endurance trials that further validate its technology.

Nova Pangaea Technologies, the UK company with a unique process to create ethanol and biochar from waste biomass for the production of carbon-negative sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), has completed successful endurance trials that further validate its technology.

The trials, which took place at its demonstration plant on Teesside, show continuous stable operation in production runs of up to 72 hours and achieved above target yields.

It marks another step forward for Nova Pangaea, which will be raising funds to progress its first commercial plant, and comes as the aviation industry seeks ways to scale up SAF production using other sustainable raw materials to end the current dependence on waste oils and fats.

Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird, an initiative supported by the UK government to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from local waste biomass to decarbonise the aviation sector. For Speedbird, Nova Pangaea will construct four UK facilities to produce bioethanol from local wastes for upgrading to SAF via LanzaJet’s Alcohol-to-Jet biorefinery.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts waste biomass and residues, such as wood chips, sawdust, or wheat straw, into ethanol, which can be used to make SAF and renewable diesel. It also produces a valuable co-product, biochar, which permanently captures carbon and makes the whole process carbon negative – removing more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases.

The latest trials used softwood residues from timber processing. Multiple runs were carried out processing up to 3 tonnes of feedstock per day.

They follow initial smaller-scale trials in early 2025 which demonstrated the viability of the process outside of the laboratory. More trials will take place next year to fine tune the design of the first commercial scale plant.

By enabling the use of waste biomass, Nova Pangaea’s process can help prevent potential shortages of SAF in the future. Under UK and EU rules, airlines must use an increasing proportion of SAF in aviation fuel – rising from 2% to as much as 70% in 2050. However, at present almost all SAF comes from used cooking oil, which is in limited supply and will not be enough to meet future demand.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), in 2030 there will be enough waste biomass available in Europe including the UK to produce around 30 million tonnes of SAF, equivalent to the European SAF targets for 2050.

Stewart Stewart, CEO of Nova Pangaea, said: “The latest trials have validated our technology and should further underpin the confidence of investors on our journey towards building our first commercial plant.

“The SAF industry is currently at a critical point. Demand is increasing and supply chain shocks such as in the Middle East show the need to find an alternative to fossil fuels, yet aviation is currently reliant on SAF from a single feedstock, which will not be enough to meet growing SAF demand.

“Nova Pangaea’s tried and tested technology offers a genuine alternative. By tapping into the plentiful supplies of waste biomass, we can boost SAF production – enhancing our energy security, and building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and revenues while reducing fossil fuel emissions.”

text:
Census figures show Hawaiʻi's population is aging faster than the national average. That's also an issue in many parts of Asia, where one government is trying a new approach to meet some of the challenges.

Singapore's government says the country has a baby problem: there aren’t enough of them.

The government wants to encourage its citizens to have more children to increase its birth rate and create a demographic cushion for its aging population.

And it's willing to spend more money to make that happen.

This past weekend, a key part of Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s National Day speech focused on child support.

The idea of a “baby bonus” at birth is not new — Singapore's government has paid one for the past 25 years.

Now, those payments will be increased — and spread out through the age of 17, including money to support the child's higher education.

Parental leave policies are also increasing, and more of the costs will be paid by the government instead of employers.

There’s even a portion related to housing.

But the Prime Minister himself says this isn't likely to by itself solve the population issue, which will continue to require immigration.

And there are mixed views from prospective parents.

A marketing firm called YouGov recently surveyed 500 young Singaporeans from their late teens to their mid-forties.

Nearly a third said there was nothing the government could do to incentivize them to have children.

text:
I started noodling on this topic with the premise that the AI genie is out of its bottle and it ain’t going back in.* So, given the concerns around AI – jobs, IP rights, slop, poor quality, users being lazy, let alone environmental and community concerns around data centers – it got me thinking: How can the ad industry sustainably use AI in marketing?

Let’s find out.

Quigley-Simpson co-founder Gerald Bagg notes that, for the most part, the environmental impact of AI is not a “routine client question” yet.

“Most organizations remain more focused on capability, speed, cost, governance and accuracy. But environmental impact will become harder to ignore as AI moves from occasional experimentation to continuous production at scale,” Bagg says.

Neil Clark, chief sustainability officer of MSQ, parent of Big Spaceship, also says it’s not a top question from clients, but he expects more clients will start asking it.

“It’s a significant topic internally,” Clark adds. “Our people raise it regularly, they want to act on it and they push us to do better. That matters because our clients’ teams are made up of the same kind of people. If our own employees are asking these questions, theirs will be too.”

What is AI’s environmental impact?

While there is some data online about the energy usage required for AI prompts and creations, many of the big players do not disclose such details or are current with it.

Let’s start small: A typical interaction on OpenAI’s ChatGPT uses about 0.3 watt-hours of electricity. Since a standard LED light bulb uses 10 watts, that AI query equates to about 2 minutes of powering the bulb.

How about images? A generative AI image takes approximately 1.2 watt hours, or the same energy as having an LED light bulb on for 7 minutes.

Video? That can take 30 to 950 watt hours, depending on quality. Looking at the higher end, creating a generative AI video can equate to leaving that light bulb on for four days.

If we compound the above information across the entire industry, that’s A LOT of light bulbs with the switch on.

With that being said, the energy to process prompts is becoming more efficient. Google says that, in May 2024, the medium Gemini prompt used 33 times more energy than it did a year later. The tech giant says software optimization, including improvements in models, contributed to the increase in energy efficiency.

Note: Scroll to the bottom to see how Ad Net Zero’s Global Media Sustainability Framework and AdGreen help measure the ad industry’s AI-related emissions.

Do consumers want AI in their advertising?

A May Bentley University-Gallup Business in Society Survey showed that 73% of US adults don’t trust businesses (either not much or not at all) to responsibly use AI. While that’s an improvement from 2023 (78%), mistrust this year is up when compared to 2025 (69%).

Let’s get closer to marketing.

One in 5 millennials has a negative view of AI’s use in marketing, which soars to nearly 2 in 5 when you ask Generation Z, per an IAB study released earlier in 2026.

When seeking an emotional connection, generative AI may not be the way to go. Kantar found that, while generative AI-created ads can spark emotion in consumers, that emotion is often not what was intended and is negative.

How about the sought-after trust factor with consumers? Klaviyo found that 31% of global consumers put less trust in a brand that uses generative AI, though 61% were neutral.

Sustainable use of AI in marketing

Getting back to the premise, there are ways today to use AI in marketing that minimize its environmental impact.

“The biggest step that you can take is the call you never make,” MSQ’s Clark says. “Plenty of tasks don’t need an AI at all, and simply asking ‘does this actually need a model?’ avoids a surprising amount.”

Clark adds that, “When something does need AI, the next question is whether it’s going to the right model, which isn’t always the smallest one. A model that’s too weak for the job just sends you round in circles regenerating answers, and that wastes far more [energy] than choosing the capable option the first time.

“Equally, reaching for the most powerful model for a task [that] a lighter one could handle is poor practice.”

Quigley-Simpson’s Bagg echoes that approach, noting that strategic thought is needed when using AI tools.

“Avoid endless generation simply to produce more alternatives. Reuse approved outputs rather than recreating them. … Reserve highly computational tools, particularly image and video generation, for situations in which they create genuine value,” Bagg says.

Bagg also says agencies and clients need to expect more from their partners.

“Organizations should also ask their technology partners for greater transparency about energy use, data-center efficiency, model size and the source of the electricity supporting their systems. Marketers cannot manage what providers do not disclose,” he says.

Clark asserts that using task-specific AI tools may be more efficient than a “general purpose giant.”

His agency took this approach with MSQ Assist, an internal AI platform. MSQ Assist “routes each task to the most appropriate model rather than defaulting to the biggest. Assist is also built on our own knowledge of our clients and is heavily templated, so it steers people towards focused, well-structured prompts and processes rather than a blank box/page every time,” Clark explains.

Sustainable considerations for adland

Today and going forward, Clark says that there are two key reasons for thinking about sustainable use of AI in advertising.

The first is simple: “AI has a real and fast-growing energy and water footprint, and marketing is adopting it at pace, so the totals mount up quickly,” Clark says.

The second leans into the important role the marketing industry plays in society.

“Marketing doesn’t only consume energy, it shapes what people see as normal and desirable. If we use AI to manufacture over consumption, or we model wasteful, throwaway AI habits ourselves, we scale that behavior across millions of people. We could just as easily do the opposite.

“Therefore, AI’s impact isn’t only about our own footprint, it’s about whether an industry with this much influence chooses to use one of the most powerful tools it has ever had thoughtfully, or not,” Clark says.

The use of AI in marketing, Bagg says, also plays into a much broader question that agencies always need to ask”

“Did this work need to be created, and did it produce enough value to justify the resources consumed?

“The more consequential and potentially controversial argument is that responsible AI use may sometimes mean deciding not to use AI at all. That challenges the prevailing assumption that greater AI adoption is inherently progress, and it is a sufficiently distinct position to warrant attention,” Bagg says.

As Clark and Bagg point out, the question about sustainable AI in marketing is not so much about the use of AI, it goes to the foundational questions that must be asked at the start of projects: What do you want to accomplish and what’s the best way to do it. And, of course, you want to do it as effectively and efficiently as possible.

* As Generation Z gets more ingrained in the workforce, it will have a say in AI usage. Also, if you disagree or have thoughts on the premise, email me.

AI impact: Ad industry resources

There are three ways that Ad Net Zero’s Global Media Sustainability Framework captures emissions from AI use: Unit operations formulae, “asset manipulation” unit operations and “corporate overhead emissions” allocation.

Ad Net Zero Global Director Jo Fenn says the framework will likely expand from creative workflow to include media delivery, optimization and other ways, including AI as a media channel.

The AdGreen Carbon Calculator measures ad production emissions and, in 2025, rolled in AI measurement. The calculator includes an Early Insights component that enables marketers to gauge the emissions impact of creative choices before being finalized.

Fenn says the tools available offer a lot of potential. “What’s exciting – and challenging – is that these show us both progress and potential. The industry is measuring more production activity than ever before, but we know we’re still only seeing a small part of the picture. Every additional production measured unlocks opportunities to reduce more emissions and save more money – without compromising creativity.”

text:
(Nova Pangea Technologies) Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) offers the opportunity to reduce our dependence on imported fossil fuels, with the price volatility and the economic impact that brings, while at the same time reducing carbon emissions from air travel. Unlike conventional jet fuel, SAF can be made from more locally available feedstocks such as forestry and agricultural residues.

Yet despite the obvious benefits, SAF still represents only a tiny fraction of global aviation fuel use and the biggest obstacle to adoption is cost. As SAF is more expensive than conventional jet fuel, airlines are concerned that it will lead to higher ticket prices.

Some airlines are now challenging the government mandates that require jet fuel to contain an increasing proportion of SAF – currently over 3% in the UK and rising to 10% in 2030.

Yet herein lies the irony. The SAF mandates will boost demand and help encourage investment in new plants – and it is only by scaling up production that we can significantly improve efficiency and bring down costs. Without doing so, prices will remain higher, supplies will be limited and nations will be trapped in the oil shock doom loop.

Clearly the price of SAF is a barrier. But how much more expensive is it than fossil-based fuel, to what extent would it affect ticket prices and how could we bring down the cost? We will look at each of these in turn.

How much does SAF cost and how does that compare to jet fuel?

The cost of SAF depends on the production method and feedstock used to make it. There are three price bands:

HEFA SAF is made from used cooking oil and waste fats and accounts for all of the SAF used today. It is also the cheapest and was approximately three times the price of jet fuel before the Iran conflict – although as the price of jet fuel rose, the gap narrowed. However with waste oils and fats in limited supply, this type of SAF can not meet growing demand – building a SAF industry will require the use of other feedstocks and processes.

SAF from waste biomass – the type produced by various conversion technologies including the Nova Pangaea process – is the next most expensive, at more than four times the price of jet fuel price before the conflict. While the technology is largely tried and tested, there are few plants as yet up and running so production is an early stage.

Electro-SAF or e-SAF uses green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide and is even more costly – it would cost more than ten times the pre-conflict price of jet fuel. This type of technology is still developing so bringing it into mass production will take some time.

Typically jet fuel accounts for around 25% of the cost of a flight. The impact of SAF on ticket prices will depend on the type of SAF and the proportion used. However to get some idea, consider the following scenario involving a £100 airline ticket where SAF is three times the cost of fossil fuel.

10% SAF: Of our £100 airline ticket, £25 represents the cost of fuel. If the airline was to replace 10% of jet fuel with SAF (the level required in 2030 under the UK rules) that would add an extra £5 to the cost of the ticket, compared with using fossil fuel alone. The ticket would cost £105.

100% SAF: If the flight was to be powered entirely using SAF (though this isn’t yet allowed under current fuel standards), fuel costs would approx triple to £75, which would increase the ticket price by £50. The ticket would cost £150.

So by using SAF, ticket prices would rise, but perhaps not to the extent that the public debate might suggest.

The 3 things that haven’t been factored in

However there are a number of factors that these price comparisons fail to take into account.

Firstly, the price of jet fuel is volatile and could rise again, with demand for air travel growing and supply chain disruptions becoming ever more frequent.

Carbon taxes imposed to reflect the cost of emissions will also effectively increase the price of fossil fuels, and so over time the price gap with SAF should narrow.

Secondly, SAF production facilities are still small compared with traditional oil refineries and do not have the economies of scale or mature supply chains that have been fine-tuned over decades in the oil industry, though this will change.

Finally, at present the price of SAF is artificially high in some cases as in practice it is linked to the price of fossil fuels, even though it is from a completely different source. Tackling these last two factors will help bring down the cost of SAF and make it a more viable option .

Bringing down the cost 1: scaling production

The most powerful way to cut costs is to scale up production. Larger plants and feedstock supply chains create economies of scale and result in greater efficiency as processes improve.

Nearly every new energy technology becomes cheaper over time – solar panels, wind turbines and batteries for example – and SAF could be expected to head in a similar direction.

Building an efficient supply chain is also important. Feedstock supplies may be patchy at the start but that will change as producers become aware of this new source of revenue and coordinate collections.

For example waste biomass largely comes from pulp and sawmills at present but there is huge potential to work with farmers, set up ‘milk rounds’ to collect crop stubble and build an agricultural supply chain. The same applies to capturing waste CO2 for e-SAF.

As demand for SAF increases, the risk is that it will drive up feedstock prices. Expanding the supply and using different feedstocks will help to keep costs down so it is important we pursue all the available SAF production technologies.

Bringing down the cost 2: decoupling prices from jet fuel

Before the Iran crisis started at the end of February 2026, jet fuel was around $750/tonne while SAF was generally over $2,000/tonne – almost three times the price. Within a matter of weeks jet fuel doubled in price to more than $1,500/tonne. In theory this should have significantly narrowed the gap, but in reality something very different happened. SAF prices rose to around £2,750/tonne – just under twice the price of fossil fuel.

Most SAF is supplied on one-year contracts and the price is tied to the cost of fossil fuels because it is a formula that buyers understand. Therefore as jet fuel rises, so do SAF prices – even though the cost of producing it is unchanged. In the short term, higher prices may be a bonus for SAF producers but in the longer term it makes SAF less competitive.

As new SAF production facilities come on stream, we have the opportunity to re-think SAF pricing structures and move to a different, less volatile system to encourage wider uptake.

Amidst global instability, energy supply chains are being weaponised and fossil fuels are no longer the cheap and reliable energy source they once were. Meanwhile oil price volatility is disrupting economic stability while carbon emissions are fuelling climate change. SAF represents a genuine alternative, albeit price is a barrier.

text:
TAIPEI, Taiwan, Aug. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EVA Air today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with leading global freight forwarder AIT Worldwide Logistics (AIT) to jointly advance EVA Air's Green Transportation Program over the next two years. In the first year of the collaboration, EVA Air will provide approximately 15,000 metric tons of CO₂e in Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) environmental attributes to Microsoft, helping reduce the Scope 3 emissions associated with air transportation of its cloud infrastructure equipment. Microsoft and Formosa Petrochemical Corporation (FPCC) also attended the signing ceremony, demonstrating a shared goal across the aviation, energy, logistics and technology sectors to accelerate lower-carbon air transportation.

The flights supporting this collaboration will depart from Taiwan using SAF supplied by FPCC. Produced from used cooking oil (UCO), the fuel has been certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) system for both its feedstock and production process. Compared with conventional jet fuel, it delivers approximately 80% lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. The associated SAF environmental attributes will be issued and retired through the ISCC Credit Transfer System (CTS), an internationally recognized registry for tracking sustainability attributes, enabling Microsoft to account for the resulting Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation.

In 2020, Microsoft committed to becoming carbon negative by 2030. To support this ambition, the company has continued to invest in SAF and other innovative solutions to reduce emissions across its value chain. This collaboration demonstrates how these investments and corporate demand can help accelerate SAF adoption while supporting the growth of Taiwan's domestic SAF market and a broader low-carbon aviation ecosystem.

As global demand for lower-carbon supply chains and sustainable transportation continues to grow, EVA Air has been actively expanding its SAF strategy. Since 2025, the airline has regularly incorporated SAF into flights departing from Asia, Europe and North America, while also signing a five-year SAF procurement agreement with FPCC. Through its Green Transportation Program, EVA Air helps corporate customers and freight forwarders better understand the carbon footprint of air transportation while supporting their Scope 3 decarbonization goals through SAF environmental attributes. Together with AIT, Microsoft and FPCC, EVA Air aims to establish a scalable and repeatable collaboration model that encourages broader corporate participation, expands SAF adoption and accelerates aviation's transition toward net zero.

"Achieving net-zero aviation requires collaboration across the entire value chain—from airlines and fuel suppliers to logistics providers and corporate customers," said Clay Sun, President of EVA Air. "This collaboration demonstrates that when customer demand is aligned with industry resources, it can accelerate the development of the SAF market. We look forward to working with more partners to make lower-carbon air transportation the new standard for global supply chains."

"Every year, our teams are shipping large volumes of sensitive, high-value air cargo from Taiwan. EVA Air has been the partner of choice to support our exponential growth in the region and our trust in their executive leadership is rooted in decades-long relationships," AIT's Chief Strategy Officer, Greg Weigel, said, "By demonstrating the benefits of this collaboration with Microsoft, a strategically important customer; EVA Air, one of our core carriers; and FPCC, a local SAF producer, we hope to influence the market and inspire similar collaborations between airlines, producers, forwarders and customers in the Asia-Pacific region."

The MOU was signed by Jason Liu, Chief Sustainability Officer of EVA Air, and Greg Weigel, Chief Strategy Officer of AIT Worldwide Logistics. The signing was witnessed by Shu-Ping Ho, Director General of Taiwan's Civil Aviation Administration; Eric Crowley, Commercial Section Deputy Chief at the American Institute in Taiwan; Clay Sun, President of EVA Air; Keh-Yen Lin, President of Formosa Petrochemical Corporation; Ryan Carter, Executive Vice President, Global Operations of AIT Worldwide Logistics; and Vincent Shih, General Manager of Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs for Microsoft Taiwan. Together, the four organizations represent an integrated SAF value chain spanning aviation, fuel production, logistics and corporate customers, further advancing supply chain decarbonization and the aviation industry's low-carbon transition.

EVA Air continues to strengthen its sustainability governance and disclosure practices. Since 2021, the airline has participated in the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) and has been included in The Sustainability Yearbook for five consecutive years. In May 2026, EVA Air also became the only Taiwanese airline selected as a constituent of the Dow Jones Best-in-Class Emerging Markets Index (DJBIC Emerging Markets Index).

The Dow Jones Best-in-Class Indices (DJBIC) are among the world's leading sustainability benchmarks, evaluating companies across environmental, social, governance and economic dimensions based on the S&P Global CSA. This recognition reflects EVA Air's continued progress in sustainability governance and decarbonization. Looking ahead, EVA Air will continue expanding the use of SAF, improving operational efficiency, and working closely with suppliers, corporate customers and global partners to accelerate the transition toward net-zero aviation and create long-term value through sustainable growth.

A Star Alliance member, EVA Air was founded in 1989 as Taiwan's first privately owned international airline. It is an affiliated company of global container-shipping leader Evergreen Line. It flies a fleet of more than 80 Boeing and Airbus aircraft to around 60 international destinations throughout Asia, Oceania, Europe, and North America. EVA Air continues to expand its global network with new routes and service enhancements, including the launch of service to Washington, D.C. (Dulles) on June 26, 2026. title: Opinion: Rural America keeps blocking data centers it desperately needs - Agri-Pulse
description:
Closed factories, the opioid epidemic, and depopulation have resulted from the “elites” forcing free trade agreements on an unsuspecting and unrepresented Middle America as good jobs have moved to China.
Even Texas Governor Greg Abbott has expressed opposition to data centers.
Data centers use water for cooling, but most will use a closed system that uses very little water once the system is charged.
(And if you didn’t post all those scary stories about data centers on social media, we wouldn’t need so many data centers!)
But, when the chance to build factories for data comes to our communities, we lose our senses.
text:
The last three presidential elections have had a common theme, mainly identified with the Trump campaigns, but certainly bipartisan in nature.

The story goes something like this: globalization has been a disaster for the little guy and trade has emptied the Midwest of people, money and opportunity. Closed factories, the opioid epidemic, and depopulation have resulted from the “elites” forcing free trade agreements on an unsuspecting and unrepresented Middle America as good jobs have moved to China.

It’s a winning political message, and echoes can be heard in the campaigns and rhetoric of politicians as far apart as Sen. Bernie Sanders, President Donald Trump, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Vice President JD Vance.

So it's surprising to me that small communities all across the country are being offered a chance to see economic growth in their communities and are turning it down. According to one recent report, local opposition has blocked or delayed at least 75 U.S. data center projects in the first three months of this year, projects that had a value of over $130 billion. New York has declared a yearlong moratorium on the construction of the facilities. Even Texas Governor Greg Abbott has expressed opposition to data centers.

Opponents mostly argue on environmental grounds: Groundwater will be depleted and poisoned, forever chemicals are used, and data centers use lots of electricity — which is, if one takes the opponents at their word, fixed in supply with no chance of hiring people to build more plants that generate more electricity.

Data centers use water for cooling, but most will use a closed system that uses very little water once the system is charged. The data center proposed near my home will use municipal wastewater, which seems to be a good solution that can be applied elsewhere. This worry about water supplies in the parts of the Midwest that experienced a very wet spring strikes me as ironic. If you wanted to attend a meeting protesting the water used by data centers in Missouri this spring, you probably had to take an alternate route to the demonstration because of roads closed by flooding and the damage high water left behind.

Computers do indeed use forever chemicals, and if that causes you angst, then get rid of your iPhone, laptop, car, and everything else in your house and business that uses semiconductors, because you are part of the problem. (And if you didn’t post all those scary stories about data centers on social media, we wouldn’t need so many data centers!)

So, we’ve voted like we are in dire economic straits, demanding radical change in carefully negotiated trade agreements to hypothetically improve our economic situation by encouraging manufacturing. We’ve damaged export markets for the main products of flyover country — corn, cotton and soybeans — in order to reshore factories. But, when the chance to build factories for data comes to our communities, we lose our senses.

My Facebook feed is full of people worrying about noise, traffic and loss of farmland. Meanwhile, farmers are promised another emergency bailout because the crops produced by that disappearing farmland can’t be sold at a profit. The school my grandchildren attend has less than half the students it did when I went to school there some fifty years ago, and plenty of houses in my small town sit empty except for the occasional raccoon and, in one case, the foxes living under the collapsing front porch.

It is important to love and protect the things that make small town and rural life special, but we will lose rural places if we continue to accept decline in the rural economy. The future can be a scary place and economic growth isn’t without growing pains. But if we look around the places we live, we have to admit that the costs of certainty, which is a continuation of our present decline, are high.

Now, after decades of watching new technologies destroy our main streets and empty our small towns, we have a chance to see our populations and our economies see some benefits from new technology. We ought not turn it down.

Blake Hurst is a farmer and greenhouse grower in northwest Missouri.

text:
The Aerobrew demonstration plant, a joint sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project of the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland and Zurich-based Metafuels, was officially inaugurated Aug. 20 on the PSI campus.

Here the production of SAF is being tested and prepared for commercialization—synthetic kerosene manufactured in what PSI said is “an exceptionally efficient way.”

From water, renewable electricity and carbon dioxide from sustainable sources, high-quality, climate-neutral aviation fuel is to be created.

This is the goal of researchers at PSI in collaboration with Metafuels.

The Aug. 20 inauguration ceremony of the Aerobrew demonstration plant on the PSI campus brought more than 150 guests from science, politics, industry and the energy sector.

With the new demonstration plant, the emerging technology is now being operated for the first time in an industrially relevant plant design.

This is a novel catalytic process for producing electro SAF that PSI researchers and the Metafuels team jointly developed and patented.

The project combines scientific research with industrial development in a targeted way to transform new findings into practical applications.

“At PSI, we conduct research for society,” said PSI Director Christian Rüegg. “The energy transition is one of the major challenges we are currently facing. The inauguration of the Aerobrew demonstration plant is an important milestone on the path to more sustainable aviation. We are proud that our cutting-edge research is making a crucial contribution to this step towards industrial production.”

From green methanol to sustainable fuel

“We have successfully developed Aerobrew together with Metafuels on a laboratory scale,” said Marco Ranocchiari, a researcher at the PSI Center for Energy and Environmental Sciences, who leads PSI’s involvement in the Aerobrew project. “With our demonstration plant, we are now testing the process under real-world conditions. This will allow us to further optimize the technology and create the conditions for industrial production.”

The new plant at PSI is designed to produce 50 liters (13.2 gallons) of SAF per day.

It is the world’s first facility to combine all the production steps for synthesizing aviation fuel from methanol under one roof, according to PSI.

“International travel and global supply chains will continue to depend on air transport,” said Saurabh Kapoor, co-founder and CEO of Metafuels. “That’s why we have developed a product that can be integrated into existing airport infrastructure and used in conventional jet engines, while at the same time significantly reducing climate-damaging emissions.”

Metafuels plans to bring the first commercial plant for production of SAF using the Aerobrew technology into operation starting in 2030.

The Aerobrew process requires no fossil fuels and achieves higher selectivity—a better yield-to-revenue ratio—compared to previously used production methods for SAF, according to PSI.

The source materials are water, from which hydrogen is produced using sustainable electricity, and carbon dioxide.

The latter can in the short term be sourced from biogenic sources such as wood or plant waste, and in the long term directly from the atmosphere.

Hydrogen and carbon dioxide are processed into green methanol.

China launches commercial SAF use in air cargo

In Ukraine, UkrAgroConsult reported that China is launching a commercial program to use sustainable aviation fuel in air cargo operations. title: The Future of High-Pressure Regulators and Valves: From Pressure Control to Operational ...
description:
As industrial organizations pursue digital transformation, operational resilience, sustainability, hydrogen adoption, and higher levels of automation, manufacturers of high-pressure regulators and valves are being challenged to deliver more than just pressure control.
Precision Pressure Control Is Becoming Increasingly Critical As industrial processes become more automated and quality requirements continue to tighten, pressure stability and control accuracy are emerging as major purchasing criteria.
As a result, pressure control accuracy is becoming as important as maximum pressure capability in many applications.
As advanced manufacturing industries continue to expand globally, demand for high-purity pressure control solutions is expected to increase significantly over the next decade.
Digitalization Is Moving into Pressure Control Industrial facilities continue to advance their digital transformation initiatives, creating new opportunities for pressure control suppliers.
text:
Beyond Pressure Ratings

For decades, the high-pressure regulator and valve market was largely defined by basic performance parameters such as pressure rating, flow capacity, and material selection. While these metrics remain important, today's industrial buyers are increasingly evaluating suppliers based on a broader set of business and operational performance indicators.

As industrial organizations pursue digital transformation, operational resilience, sustainability, hydrogen adoption, and higher levels of automation, manufacturers of high-pressure regulators and valves are being challenged to deliver more than just pressure control. End users are seeking solutions that improve reliability, reduce lifecycle costs, enhance safety, support decarbonization initiatives, and provide measurable operational value.

As ARC continues its research into the global high-pressure regulator and valve market, discussions with suppliers increasingly center on several key performance indicators (KPIs) that have emerged as the primary drivers of competitive differentiation.

Reliability Has Become the New Currency

In today's operating environment, unplanned downtime can have a significantly greater financial impact than the initial cost of a valve or regulator. Consequently, reliability has become one of the most important factors influencing supplier selection.

Manufacturers are focusing on extended service life, reduced maintenance requirements, improved sealing technologies, and enhanced product durability to help customers maximize asset availability. Whether in hydrogen fueling stations, semiconductor manufacturing facilities, chemical plants, or offshore production platforms, operators increasingly prioritize solutions that improve uptime and reduce operational risk. Suppliers that can demonstrate long-term field performance, proven installed bases, and lifecycle value are often better positioned than those competing solely on technical specifications.

Precision Pressure Control Is Becoming Increasingly Critical

As industrial processes become more automated and quality requirements continue to tighten, pressure stability and control accuracy are emerging as major purchasing criteria.

Applications such as semiconductor gas delivery, specialty gas management, laboratory operations, hydrogen fuel systems, and advanced manufacturing often require extremely stable outlet pressure regardless of fluctuations in inlet pressure or process demand. Manufacturers are investing in improved sensing technologies, advanced regulator designs, and intelligent pressure management capabilities to meet these requirements. As a result, pressure control accuracy is becoming as important as maximum pressure capability in many applications.

Safety and Leak Integrity Remain Top Priorities

The growing use of hydrogen, specialty gases, toxic chemicals, and high-value process fluids is elevating the importance of leak-tight performance.

Regulatory requirements, environmental initiatives, and corporate sustainability programs are increasing scrutiny around fugitive emissions and process safety. End users are placing greater emphasis on sealing performance, emissions compliance, material compatibility, and product testing procedures. Manufacturers that can demonstrate exceptional leak integrity, robust testing protocols, and proven performance in hazardous applications are seeing increased interest across multiple industries.

Hydrogen Is Redefining Product Development Priorities

Few market trends are generating as much attention as hydrogen. Investments in hydrogen production, storage, transportation, and fueling infrastructure are creating new requirements for pressure control technologies.

Unlike traditional industrial gases, hydrogen introduces unique challenges related to permeation, embrittlement, sealing integrity, and high-pressure operation. As a result, suppliers are accelerating investments in hydrogen-compatible materials, specialized regulator designs, and safety-focused engineering practices. Many industry participants now see hydrogen readiness as a strategic differentiator, not just another application area.

High Purity Is Expanding Beyond Semiconductor Applications

Historically associated with semiconductor manufacturing, high-purity requirements are increasingly appearing across life sciences, biotechnology, specialty chemicals, energy, and advanced industrial gas applications.

Customers are paying closer attention to particle generation, surface finish quality, contamination control, cleanroom manufacturing practices, and material traceability. These factors are becoming essential considerations during supplier selection. As advanced manufacturing industries continue to expand globally, demand for high-purity pressure control solutions is expected to increase significantly over the next decade.

Customization Continues to Create Competitive Advantage

Although many industrial customers seek standardized solutions, a growing number of applications require highly specialized products.

Hydrogen fueling systems, aerospace platforms, defense applications, subsea installations, specialty gas systems, and research facilities often present operating conditions that cannot be addressed through standard catalog offerings. Manufacturers that combine strong engineering resources with application expertise are increasingly differentiating themselves through customized solutions. In many cases, engineering support and application knowledge have become as valuable as the hardware itself.

Digitalization Is Moving into Pressure Control

Industrial facilities continue to advance their digital transformation initiatives, creating new opportunities for pressure control suppliers.

Customers are beginning to evaluate how regulators and valves can contribute to broader operational objectives such as predictive maintenance, remote asset monitoring, diagnostics, and performance optimization. While digital adoption remains in the early stages for much of the regulator market, suppliers that develop intelligent pressure management capabilities may gain a meaningful competitive advantage as industrial connectivity expands.

Lifecycle Services and Recurring Revenue

Leading suppliers are using aftermarket services, maintenance agreements, field support, and asset lifecycle management to strengthen customer relationships and create recurring revenue streams. These offerings are shifting supplier differentiation beyond equipment performance and toward long-term service value and customer support.

AI-Driven Operations and Asset Intelligence

Manufacturers are also exploring smart pressure management solutions that combine sensors, diagnostics, connectivity, and analytics. Over time, AI-enabled monitoring can help operators make better maintenance decisions, improve safety, optimize equipment utilization, and transform pressure-control assets into sources of operational intelligence.

Future Growth Opportunities by End Market

Growth opportunities are expanding across end markets that require higher levels of purity, reliability, precision, and safety. AI infrastructure, semiconductor capacity expansion, LNG, carbon capture, renewable natural gas, sustainable aviation fuel, industrial gases, aerospace and defense, nuclear energy, and advanced manufacturing are all creating new demand for advanced pressure-control solutions.

Global Support, Supply Chain Resilience, and Localization

Technical performance alone does not guarantee market success. End users increasingly value suppliers that can provide strong engineering support, rapid response times, application expertise, and global service capabilities. As manufacturing operations become increasingly globalized, customers often prefer suppliers capable of supporting projects consistently across multiple regions. This trend favors manufacturers with extensive technical resources, established distribution networks, and strong customer support organizations.

The ability to provide local expertise while maintaining global consistency is becoming an important market differentiator. Customers are increasingly evaluating suppliers based on manufacturing footprint diversity, supply chain resilience, and the ability to support regional sourcing initiatives.

The Competitive Landscape Is Evolving

Across these applications, the market is moving toward suppliers that can combine engineering depth, proven reliability, digital capabilities, and strong application support. This shift will influence how manufacturers position their portfolios, differentiate their offerings, and prioritize investment over the next decade.

ARC's upcoming High-Pressure Regulators Market Research will examine which end markets are driving demand, how competitive differentiation is evolving, where suppliers are investing for growth, and which technologies are reshaping the industry's competitive landscape.

The next blog in this series will take a closer look at reliability as an increasingly important performance metric for high-pressure regulators and valves and explore a critical question for suppliers and end users alike: How much is downtime worth?

Related ARC Insights

ARC has also examined developments in hydrogen production, pressure control, gas management, and emerging energy infrastructure that are relevant to the evolving high-pressure regulator market:

Transitioning to a Hydrogen Ecosystem

Hydrogen Production: A Sustainable Market Segment with over Proportional Growth Expectations for Control Equipment

These insights provide additional perspective on the growth of hydrogen applications, the need for stable and reliable pressure management, and the expanding role of pressure-control technologies in emerging energy and industrial markets.

For centuries, Mexico has capitalized on growing and harvesting a plant often distilled into Tequila or Mezcal. It’s called agave and it thrives on little water and a lot of heat. Now, with a California law restricting water use on farms, Valley farmers are looking to agave as a new revenue stream on their land, and working to localize supply.

California’s highest court is weighing whether a sheriff broke the law when he seized hundreds of thousands of ballots earlier this year. The court heard oral arguments Monday.

The Trump administration has ended a long standing agreement that kept ICE out of workplaces that are being investigated by the U.S. Department of Labor.

When James Hunt planted 14 acres of agave on his secluded Merced farm last year, he thought he’d harvest it for liquor. But then he did more research on the large spiky succulent, and that dream snowballed.

“You could have spirits, agave syrup, agave inulin, biofuel, sustainable aviation fuel,” says Hunt.

He knew these ideas needed an industry in the US, so he started preaching the gospel of agave he says, to anyone who would listen.

“I was a farm manager, farm operator, and now I’m an industry advocate, trying to build out something that I think can have a lot of benefit for small farms in general,” says Hunt.

Hunt knows many growers who are testing out agave right now, but it’s not just for kicks. It’s also out of necessity, and it has to do with groundwater.

Josh Viers is a professor of civil and environmental engineering at U-C Merced. “We’re taking more water out than is going back in,” he says.

Viers is describing groundwater overdraft. That happens when groundwater gets taken out, but not replenished. It dries wells and sinks land.

So in 2014, California legislators enacted a law called the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, or SGMA to stabilize water use.

“It gave them a drawdown period over 30 years to be able to meet that sustainability target, and also to maintain some specific guardrails, you might say, about that use,” says Viers.

SGMA created local agencies to gradually limit the use of the water. That means farmers are making cuts, like watering a few inches of soil on crops like agave instead of a few feet of soil on an almond tree.

Some farmers, are more equipped than others.

Omar Ramirez is a grower in Le Grand – a community in southeast Merced County, but he also owns a Tequila line based in Mexico called Luna Yena.

“A lot of my businesses have arose from problems and there’s a common saying that if you know how to solve people’s problems, you’re always going to have work,” says Ramirez.

He lived in Mexico for a few years as a kid. In Le Grand he used to grow almonds, until profits tanked a few years ago. With SGMA in focus, he thought, ‘Why not try something familiar?’

He planted 100 acres of agave.

“As a Mexican myself, Mexican American, that light bulb lit to say, ‘Hey, you know what? I think this is a perfect way to bring both of my cultures that I really love into one location.’

He’s excited about conversations that go beyond alcohol. He might make spirits, but he’s also looking at animal feed and building materials.

He says opportunities that arise in the United States are a bit different than what are destined in Mexico.

Hunt also feels good about agave’s destiny here. Nearly all of his plants survived the winter frost, even though some have dried up tips.

It’ll be four to six years before the first batch are ready to harvest, and he’ll spend that time trying to develop the agave economy.

“Farming is a gamble,” says Hunt. “And I’m willing to go out on a limb for this because I believe in it.”

He’s lived on this land his whole life, and he’ll do whatever it takes to keep it.

But Sonni Waknin, an attorney for the plaintiffs who spoke after the hearing, says a warrant doesn’t trump California election code. Not even an elected sheriff has the power to ignore election rules and seize cast ballots outside the view of the public.

The showdown comes as California’s expansive system of vote-by-mail faces attacks not only from President Donald Trump, who has labeled mail balloting a form of cheating, but also from local election officials aligned with the president.

title: Why Are Wood Fiber Costs So High for European Pulp Producers? - ResourceWise
description:
Wood fiber is the largest component of manufacturing cash costs for many European pulp producers.
Europe's high wood fiber costs are not the result of a single market factor.
Competition for European Wood Fiber Is Increasing Pulp producers increasingly compete for wood with industries outside traditional pulp and paper markets.
What Can European Pulp Producers Do About High Fiber Costs?
Gain Deeper Insight into Global Wood Fiber Markets For pulp producers, suppliers, and investors, understanding regional fiber availability and delivered wood costs is increasingly important for evaluating competitiveness and making strategic decisions.
text:
European pulp producers face some of the highest wood fiber costs in the world due to a combination of constrained wood supply, growing competition for forest-based feedstocks, elevated log prices, changing trade flows, and regulatory pressures.

For pulp mills, these conditions have made fiber an increasingly important factor in overall production economics. In several major European pulp-producing countries, wood fiber now represents well over half of manufacturing cash costs—and in some markets, more than 70%.

Understanding what is driving those costs is essential for producers evaluating procurement strategies, mill competitiveness, and future investment.

How Much of a European Pulp Mill's Manufacturing Cost Comes from Wood Fiber?

Wood fiber is the largest component of manufacturing cash costs for many European pulp producers.

ResourceWise's WoodMarket Prices (WMP) data shows that wood fiber accounted for more than 70% of manufacturing cash costs for pulp producers in Austria and Finland in Q4 2025. Those elevated ratios continued into Q1 2026.

Across several major European markets:

Austria: Wood fiber reached approximately 73% of manufacturing cash costs in Q4 2025.

Finland: Fiber remained above 70%, despite easing from previous highs.

Sweden: Wood fiber represented approximately 64–67% of manufacturing cash costs.

Germany: Fiber's share increased from approximately 49% in early 2024 to nearly 57% by early 2026.

Source: WoodMarket Prices

These percentages vary by mill and product mix. Market pulp production, for example, is particularly exposed to wood fiber costs, while mills producing grades that use more fillers may have a lower percentage of their manufacturing costs tied directly to wood.

Temporary increases in wood availability can also influence these figures. Storm damage and other forest disturbances have periodically increased European wood supply and reduced costs, but those effects are temporary.

Learn More About WoodMarket Prices

Why Are Wood Fiber Costs So High in Europe?

Europe's high wood fiber costs are not the result of a single market factor. Instead, several structural pressures are affecting both the availability and price of pulpwood, logs, and wood chips.

1. Competition for European Wood Fiber Is Increasing

Pulp producers increasingly compete for wood with industries outside traditional pulp and paper markets.

Bioenergy, renewable fuels, engineered wood products, and biomaterials all rely on forest-based feedstocks. As these industries grow, more buyers can compete for the same underlying wood resource.

Policy can also influence this competition. Renewable-energy and fuel mandates can create demand for certain forest-derived feedstocks, allowing competing applications to support higher prices even when feedstock costs increase.

At the same time, European pulp producers have less flexibility in some traditional sourcing channels. The loss of Russian wood imports has been particularly important for Baltic and Nordic markets, including Finland, tightening regional supply and increasing dependence on other sources.

2. Log Prices Remain Well Above Historical Averages

European softwood log prices remain substantially above their 2020 levels.

ResourceWise WoodMarket Prices data shows that delivered softwood roundwood prices in Germany during 2025 were approximately 66% higher than in 2020. Finland and Sweden both recorded prices roughly 50% above 2020 levels.

There are signs of stabilization in some individual markets.

Finland's softwood pulp log prices, for example, declined approximately 17% from their Q2 2025 peak. Austria's pulp log prices also stabilized following several quarters of declines.

However, lower prices compared with recent peaks do not necessarily mean a return to historically normal costs.

Other fiber categories remain elevated. Softwood chip prices continued increasing through 2025 in Austria and Germany, while French chip prices flattened in early 2026 but remained at relatively high levels.

Longer-term wood availability is another consideration. Dry summers, high temperatures, and other forest disturbances can affect future conifer supply. Some European forest-products companies are also looking beyond their domestic markets to secure long-term access to wood resources.

3. Regulatory Changes Add Additional Pressure

European pulp and paper producers operate within an evolving regulatory environment that can affect both manufacturing costs and future wood availability.

Important policies include:

The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)

The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)

The EU Nature Restoration Regulation

The impact is not limited to direct compliance costs.

Changes to forest-management requirements can influence the amount of wood available for commercial use, while energy and emissions policies affect production economics and competition for forest-based resources.

Proposed changes to ETS benchmarks have also raised concerns about future investment. CEPI estimates that proposed benchmark reductions could reduce annual investment capacity for Europe's pulp and paper industry by approximately €1 billion, potentially affecting investment in mill modernization and decarbonization.

Restoration policies could also reduce the amount of forest available for commercial harvesting over time. If supply becomes more constrained, pulp mills may face additional competition for available wood.

How Do Energy Costs Affect Wood Fiber Prices?

Energy costs influence fiber economics before wood ever reaches a pulp mill.

Higher fuel prices increase the cost of harvesting and transporting wood, while elevated energy and chemical costs add pressure within the mill itself. This means producers can face higher costs across several stages of production simultaneously.

As a result, fiber prices need to be viewed within Europe's broader manufacturing cost environment rather than as an isolated procurement expense.

What Is the Outlook for European Wood Fiber Prices?

European wood fiber prices may fluctuate from quarter to quarter, but several structural factors suggest costs are likely to remain elevated relative to historical levels.

These include continued competition from bioenergy and biomaterials, limited growth in available wood supply, regulatory and sustainability requirements, transportation and energy costs, and uncertainty surrounding international fiber trade.

Recycling trends add another dimension to Europe's fiber balance. Policies that encourage greater use of recycled material can increase demand for recovered fiber, but recycling cannot eliminate the need for virgin fiber. Fiber is lost and degraded during repeated recycling cycles, meaning virgin wood fiber remains necessary to maintain the overall fiber system.

If paper and pulp demand strengthens, wood suppliers may respond by increasing harvest activity where possible. However, stronger demand could also intensify competition for an already constrained resource.

For European pulp producers, this means wood procurement will remain an important part of maintaining mill competitiveness.

What Can European Pulp Producers Do About High Fiber Costs?

Producers cannot control many of the structural forces affecting Europe's wood markets, but they can improve how they respond to them.

That starts with understanding how delivered wood costs vary across regions, fiber types, and competing markets. Producers can use regional pricing and supply data to benchmark procurement costs, identify changes in local fiber availability, evaluate alternative sourcing regions, and understand how their fiber position compares with competing mills.

As fiber represents a growing share of manufacturing costs, procurement intelligence becomes increasingly important to broader mill strategy.

Gain Deeper Insight into Global Wood Fiber Markets

For pulp producers, suppliers, and investors, understanding regional fiber availability and delivered wood costs is increasingly important for evaluating competitiveness and making strategic decisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is wood fiber so expensive in Europe?

Wood fiber prices are elevated because European pulp producers face constrained supply, competition from other forest-based industries, historically high log prices, reduced flexibility in international sourcing, and regulatory and energy-related pressures.

Which European countries have the highest wood fiber cost exposure?

ResourceWise data shows particularly high wood fiber shares in Austria and Finland, where fiber represented more than 70% of manufacturing cash costs in late 2025. Sweden also remained high at approximately 64–67%.

Are European wood fiber prices falling?

Some markets have eased from recent peaks, but prices generally remain elevated compared with historical levels. Finland's softwood pulp log prices, for example, declined from their Q2 2025 peak while remaining well above 2020 levels.

Why does bioenergy affect pulpwood prices?

Pulp mills and bioenergy producers can compete for overlapping forest resources. Policies supporting renewable energy and fuels can increase demand for forest-based feedstocks, adding competition within regional wood markets.

Does recycled fiber reduce demand for virgin wood fiber?

Recycling can reduce the amount of virgin fiber required for certain paper and packaging products, but it cannot replace virgin fiber entirely. Fibers degrade and are lost through successive recycling cycles, requiring new virgin fiber to enter the system.

text:
The future of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) will depend on strong partnerships among farmers, fuel producers, the aviation industry and government leaders, according to panelists participating in a discussion during the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit in the St. Louis region. During a session titled “The Future of Flight Runs on SAF,” attendees heard how Illinois, Missouri and the broader Midwest corn belt are positioned to play a leading role in expanding domestic SAF production while creating new opportunities for agricultural producers and strengthening the aviation industry.

Moderated by Darren James, director of MidAmerica St. Louis Airport, the panel featured Jim Hedges, CEO of CoverCress, an ag-tech company developing a winter oilseed crop grown between corn and soybean seasons, and Cindy Tomei, president of the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII). The discussion focused on the current state of the SAF industry, the need for investment in production and infrastructure, and the critical role agriculture will play in meeting growing demand for lower-carbon aviation fuels.

“Illinois has emerged as a leader in the SAF space, with industry, government and research organizations collaborating to attract projects and advance the sector,” Tomei said.

She discussed how the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII) was established in Illinois two years ago following a state-led SAF summit convened at the governor's request. That event brought together stakeholders from across the aviation fuel ecosystem and highlighted the need for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)-specific testing standards, technical expertise and workforce training. She said, today, the Institute, which is headquartered in Sugar Grove, Illinois, serves as a hub for SAF education, testing and industry collaboration. It provides hands-on laboratory training in fuel testing, helps organizations understand SAF properties and blending considerations, and connects stakeholders across the global SAF supply chain.

Discussing recent progress in the SAF industry, Tomei said it has been accelerated by greater clarity around the federal 45Z tax credit and improvements in calculating carbon intensity scores, which help determine incentive eligibility.

At the same time, growing global demand, including sustainable aviation fuel mandates across the European Union and continuing challenges moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz, has increased awareness of SAF and heightened the urgency to scale production and deployment. As demand for sustainable aviation fuel continues to accelerate, Tomei said it’s increasingly important to build the infrastructure needed to move fuel from production facilities to airports. She noted that O'Hare is in one of the top 10 airports for SAF procurement worldwide.

“Speed is really of the essence, whether it is getting SAF scaled up regardless of what the feedstock is, but also having the right infrastructure to get it transported, stored and blended with jet fuel, so that it can actually be used,” Tomei said.

The panel also highlighted the important role Midwest agriculture can play in supporting SAF and other renewable fuel feedstock production. Hedges, whose company continued to hit significant milestones over the past year, noted that meeting future demand will require additional feedstocks and innovative crops that can complement existing farming operations while providing new revenue opportunities from existing acreage for producers.

“I see a huge role for Midwest agriculture,” Hedges said. “We’re crushing so many soybean acres already, but there’s no new soybean acres coming in. As all types of renewable fuels use continue to grow, we need to have supply to fulfill the demand. You have to have these new types of crops... canola, camelina, as well as CoverCress. These are crops that are planted when ground is fallow so they are truly additive to the supply of feedstock. We want everybody to be successful, because I think our biggest challenge is not meeting the demand.”

The discussion underscored how emerging feedstocks and technologies can position farmers as increasingly important participants in the future aviation fuel supply chain. Hedges explained the importance of raising awareness about the opportunity to easily grow an additional crop between corn and soybean seasons, creating a new revenue stream for farmers while improving soil health. Panelists noted that continued innovation, adoption of new crops and closer coordination throughout the production process will be essential to scaling the SAF and other renewable fuels industry.

Hedges stressed that collaboration across the fuel production ecosystem must begin early in the development process, particularly because federal Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) pathway approvals can take years. Hedges noted that CoverCress Inc just hit a major milestone with obtaining the first RFS pathway approval for CoverCress Oil, which took 2.5 years from the time the pathway was submitted.

“The earlier coordination with refiners can begin with these new crops, the better,” Hedges said. “Establish a relationship with one or more refiners. Get your pathways going as you’re doing your product development. And that way, when the product is commercially viable, it’s probably going to be around the time that you get these RFS pathway approvals.”

Panelists also discussed the rigorous testing and quality controls required for aviation fuels, the need for supportive public policies and the importance of ensuring adequate production capacity. The conversation reinforced that SAF development is not solely an aviation initiative, but one that relies on coordination among agriculture, energy, transportation and economic development stakeholders.

Looking ahead, Tomei encouraged greater collaboration among the many organizations already advancing SAF initiatives throughout Illinois. “Illinois really is a leader,” Tomei said. “There are so many good things happening in different pockets on an individual basis with SAF that, if we brought it together, we’d be an even stronger powerhouse.”

For farmers and agricultural organizations, the growth of SAF represents an opportunity to help supply a developing domestic fuel market through both established commodities and new crops, supporting farm revenue, sustainability goals and domestic energy security. “Right now, we're all kind of in that early ramp up stage, but we are planning to have hundreds of thousands of acres of these new innovative crops by the early 2030s,” Hedges said.

The second annual Global Aerospace Summit brought together aerospace manufacturers, suppliers and leaders in military, cargo movement, transportation, economic development and other sectors for a two-day program focused on advancing innovation and strengthening the industry’s future.
