text:
The global energy transition is creating strong demand for low-carbon fuels that can reduce emissions in sectors where direct electrification remains difficult. Among the technologies gaining momentum, e-fuels also known as electrofuels or synthetic fuels are emerging as an important pathway for decarbonizing aviation, shipping, heavy-duty transportation, chemicals, and other energy-intensive industries.

Green hydrogen electrolyzers are emerging as a critical technology in the e-fuels industry, enabling renewable electricity and water to be converted into hydrogen, the key energy input for producing synthetic fuels. E-fuels, also known as electrofuels or power-to-fuels, are produced by combining hydrogen generated from renewable electricity with a carbon source such as captured CO2.

How Green Hydrogen Electrolyzers Enable E-fuel Production

The e-fuel production chain typically begins with renewable electricity from solar, wind, or other low-carbon sources. An electrolyzer uses this electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The resulting green hydrogen is then combined with captured CO2 and converted into synthetic fuels

Renewable Electricity → Electrolyzer → Green Hydrogen → CO2 + H2 → Synthesis → E-fuel

Depending on the synthesis pathway, the output can include e-methanol, e-diesel, e-gasoline, e-kerosene/e-SAF, and other synthetic fuels.

E-fuels Industry Growth:

The E-fuels Industry is gaining momentum because governments and companies are looking for scalable solutions to reduce emissions from hard-to-abate sectors.

Several factors are supporting industry growth:

Increasing decarbonization targets across transportation and industrial sectors

Expansion of renewable power generation

Rapid development of green hydrogen production

Growing investment in electrolyzers and Power-to-Liquid technologies

Rising demand for low-carbon aviation and marine fuels

Development of carbon capture and utilization technologies

Government incentives and low-carbon fuel mandates

Increasing corporate commitments toward net-zero emissions

Aviation, shipping, and heavy-duty transport as important areas of demand because these sectors face technical or economic challenges in adopting direct electrification.

E-Fuels Market Size

According to MarketsandMarkets, the global e-fuels market is projected to grow from USD 24.49 billion in 2025 to USD 66.25 billion by 2030, registering a CAGR of 22.0%. The growth is being supported by demand for sustainable alternatives to fossil fuels, stricter emissions standards, supportive low-carbon fuel policies, and the need to decarbonize hard-to-electrify sectors.

Why Electrolyzers Are Critical to the E-fuels Industry

The electrolyzer is more than simply a hydrogen-generation unit—it is one of the central components determining the cost, efficiency, scalability, and carbon intensity of an e-fuel plant.

A major advantage of electrolysis is that hydrogen production can be directly coupled with renewable power. PEM electrolyzers, for example, can respond rapidly to changes in electricity availability, while alkaline electrolyzers offer commercial maturity and SOEC technology can potentially benefit from high-temperature heat integration.

As a result, advances in electrolyzer efficiency, durability, operating flexibility, and manufacturing scale can have a direct impact on the economics of e-fuel production.

The global electrolyzers market is expanding rapidly as governments and industries invest in green hydrogen production. MarketsandMarkets projects the electrolyzers market to grow from USD 2.08 billion in 2025 to USD 14.48 billion by 2031, at a CAGR of 38.2%.

Electrolyzers and E-SAF Production

One of the most important applications is e-SAF (electro-sustainable aviation fuel). In a power-to-liquid pathway, renewable electricity powers an electrolyzer to produce hydrogen. Hydrogen is then combined with CO2 to produce syngas or methanol, which can subsequently be converted into aviation fuel through Fischer–Tropsch or methanol-to-jet pathways.

This makes electrolyzers particularly important for aviation decarbonization because long-distance aviation requires energy-dense fuels and cannot easily rely solely on direct electrification.

Electrolyzers and E-Methanol

Green hydrogen is also a fundamental feedstock for e-methanol. Captured CO2 is hydrogenated using renewable hydrogen to produce methanol, which can be used as a low-carbon fuel or as an intermediate for producing other synthetic fuels.

E-methanol is attracting attention in the maritime sector, where shipping companies are exploring alternative fuels to reduce dependence on conventional marine fuels. It can also serve as an intermediate for producing synthetic aviation fuels and other hydrocarbons.

Electrolyzer Technologies for E-fuel Production

Different electrolyzer technologies can serve different e-fuel plant configurations:

PEM electrolyzers: Suitable for projects requiring fast response to variable renewable electricity.

Alkaline electrolyzers: Offer established commercial technology and are widely considered for large-scale hydrogen production.

Solid oxide electrolyzers (SOECs): Operate at high temperatures and can potentially use available process heat to improve overall system efficiency.

The e-fuel industry is likely to evaluate electrolyzers not only on hydrogen production cost but also on electricity utilization, dynamic operation, system integration, lifetime, maintenance, and access to renewable power.

E-fuels Market Growth Creates Opportunities for Electrolyzer Manufacturers

The expansion of the e-fuels industry creates a parallel opportunity for electrolyzer manufacturers.

Electrolyzer companies including thyssenkrupp nucera, Siemens Energy, John Cockerill, Nel, and Cummins are among prominent players in the electrolyzers market.

Outlook for the E-fuels Industry

The e-fuels industry and green hydrogen electrolyzers are closely interconnected. E-fuels provide a potential decarbonization pathway for sectors where direct electrification is difficult, while electrolyzers provide the green hydrogen required for many synthetic fuel production routes.

For aviation, shipping, heavy transport, and other hard-to-abate sectors, e-fuels can potentially provide energy-dense fuels while leveraging existing fuel-handling and engine infrastructure. However, their competitiveness will depend on falling renewable electricity and electrolyzer costs, higher conversion efficiency, reliable CO2 sourcing, supportive regulations, and large-scale project deployment.

The global e-fuels industry projected to reach USD 66.25 billion by 2030 and the electrolyzers market expected to reach USD 14.48 billion by 2031, the intersection between green hydrogen and synthetic fuels is positioned to become an increasingly important part of the global energy transition.

SOUTHLAKE, Texas, Aug. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- American EcoFuels Inc. Expanding an Existing Intellectual Property Foundation

The documentation also identifies pending U.S. Application No. 18/922,441 and related international applications or filings involving Canada, Europe, Mexico, Japan, South Africa and a PCT application.

A second patent family identified in the assignment documentation includes U.S. Patent No. 11,471,853 and associated U.S. Application No. 17/687,640, together with an additional U.S. application and PCT filing. Management believes that developing a broad intellectual property portfolio around the Company's integrated technology platform could become an important strategic asset as American EcoFuels progresses through engineering, testing, certification and commercialization.

American EcoFuels' technology strategy is based on converting carbon-containing feedstocks, including natural gas and coal, into synthesis gas and subsequently engineering that molecular building material into high-value synthetic hydrocarbons. The Company's principal focus includes technologies intended to produce SAF, SPK and other high-performance liquid fuels through integrated GTL and CTL processes utilizing proprietary catalysts and related process technologies.

Rather than seeking intellectual property protection around a single piece of equipment or individual process step, the Company's broader strategy is intended to establish protection around multiple aspects of an integrated technology platform, including different processes, configurations, feedstocks, improvements and potential end products. American EcoFuels believes this approach could ultimately support multiple commercialization models, including Company-owned or jointly developed production facilities, strategic partnerships with organizations controlling feedstocks and infrastructure, collaborations with aviation and industrial customers, and potential licensing of elements of the Company's technology to third-party operators. A licensing strategy could potentially provide the Company with an opportunity to participate economically in multiple facilities without independently financing and constructing each production plant.

Brent Nelson, Director of American EcoFuels and Chief Executive Officer of Kepler GTL Technologies Inc., stated, "Our intellectual property strategy is about protecting a technology platform, not simply an individual fuel product. The Phase 2 program is intended to significantly expand the protection surrounding that platform as we move from technology development toward engineering, testing, certification and commercialization."

text:
Nova Pangaea Technologies, the UK company with a unique process to create sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from waste biomass, has completed successful endurance trials that further validate its technology.

The trials, which took place at its demonstration plant on Teesside, show continuous stable operation in production runs of up to 72 hours and achieved above target yields.

It marks another step forward for Nova Pangaea, which will be raising funds to progress its first commercial plant, and comes as the aviation industry seeks ways to scale up SAF production using other sustainable raw materials to end the current dependence on waste oils and fats.

Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird, an initiative supported by the UK government to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from local waste biomass to decarbonize the aviation sector. For Speedbird, Nova Pangaea will construct four UK facilities to produce bioethanol from local wastes for upgrading to SAF.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts waste biomass and residues, such as wood chips, sawdust, or wheat straw, into ethanol, which can be used to make SAF and renewable diesel. It also produces a valuable co-product, biochar, which permanently captures carbon and makes the whole process carbon negative - removing more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases.

The latest trials used softwood residues from timber processing. Multiple runs were carried out processing up to 3 tons of feedstock per day.

They follow initial smaller-scale trials in early 2025 which demonstrated the viability of the process outside of the laboratory. More trials will take place next year to fine tune the design of the first commercial scale plant.

By enabling the use of waste biomass, Nova Pangaea’s process can help prevent potential shortages of SAF in the future. Under UK and EU rules, airlines must use an increasing proportion of SAF in aviation fuelrising from 2% to as much as 70% in 2050. However, at present almost all SAF comes from used cooking oil, which is in limited supply and will not be enough to meet future demand.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), in 2030 there will be enough waste biomass available in Europe including the UK to produce around 30 million tons of SAF, equivalent to the European SAF targets for 2050.

Stewart Stewart, CEO of Nova Pangaea, said: “The latest trials have validated our technology and should further underpin the confidence of investors on our journey towards building our first commercial plant.

“The SAF industry is currently at a critical point. Demand is increasing and supply chain shocks such as in the Middle East show the need to find an alternative to fossil fuels, yet aviation is currently reliant on SAF from a single feedstock, which will not be enough to meet growing SAF demand.

“Nova Pangaea’s tried and tested technology offers a genuine alternative. By tapping into the plentiful supplies of waste biomass, we can boost SAF production – enhancing our energy security, and building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and revenues while reducing fossil fuel emissions.”

Nova Pangaea has raised over £21 m to date from investors, including International Airlines Group, PXN Ventures, Mercia Ventures and the first Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund, alongside UK government grant funding awarded under the Advanced Fuels Fund competition.

text:
Waste from food production or wood processing can be turned into a biofuel for more sustainable air travel. The raw oil, however, is unstable and difficult to use. A Swedish research team is working on optimising the refining process.

Biofuel has the potential to make transport and air travel more sustainable, but only if it is produced in a certain way. The research team behind the study includes members of CESTAP, a competence centre for biofuels for turbines, which focuses on sustainable fuels for air travel and power generation. The sustainability of biofuels is a complex issue with many factors to consider. The raw products used should be waste from other processes, and all other fuels required to produce them must be accounted for.

The first step in biofuel production is to heat the waste in a process called pyrolysis, turning it into a liquid called pyrolysis oil. However, pyrolysis oil should not be used directly. It is unstable, viscous and not very efficient as a fuel. Therefore, a second refining step is needed, and that is where the recent research comes in. The pyrolysis oil is mixed with materials that combine to form particles, then heated again in a hydrogen atmosphere. The goal is to reduce its oxygen content, making it easier and more efficient to use.

The particles that form act as catalysts, meaning they are added to speed up a chemical process that would otherwise be too slow to be practical. Forming the most efficient, or active, catalytic particles is quite a finicky task, where even their atomic-scale structure plays a role. X-ray methods are essential for understanding how the particles work and how they can be further optimised.

“The study provided a detailed characterisation under realistic process conditions, and demonstrated that both the biomass composition and the process conditions play a crucial role in determining the structure of the active particles,” says Sara Blomberg, one of the researchers. “Since the particles are formed inside the reactor, knowing which reactor conditions generate maximally active catalyst particles is important for further optimising the industrial process.”

One important process the researchers are looking into is whether there are circumstances under which the catalyst deactivates and stops working.

“We were interested in characterising feedstock contaminants that might potentially contribute to catalyst deactivation,” says Sara Blomberg. “We were able to map contaminants in the nanoparticles with high sensitivity, and the analysis provided important insights into possible catalyst deactivation.”

The researchers compared catalyst particles formed in a model hydrocarbon fuel to those formed in the real industrial process to see what differences would result from the more complex conditions.

“The most important finding from the study was that the active particles differed significantly when the particles were formed in biomass-derived feedstock. Both the biomass itself and the large-scale pilot plant conditions appeared to strongly influence the particle formation and resulting morphology,” concludes Blomberg. “Our findings highlight the importance of characterising catalysts not only under ideal laboratory conditions, but also in scaled-up processes where the catalyst is exposed to more complex environments.”

text:
A UK process for converting waste biomass into feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) has completed continuous production runs lasting up to 72 hours, as its developer prepares to raise funding for a first commercial-scale plant.

Nova Pangaea Technologies carried out the endurance trials at its demonstration facility on Teesside, where its REFNOVA process operated continuously for periods of up to three days.

The company said the trials achieved above-target yields while demonstrating stable continuous operation. Multiple runs were completed using softwood residues from timber processing, with the plant handling up to three tonnes of feedstock per day.

The results follow smaller-scale trials conducted in early 2025 and represent another step in moving the technology from demonstration towards commercial deployment. Further trials are planned for 2027 to refine the design of Nova Pangaea’s first commercial plant.

From residues to fuel

REFNOVA converts lignocellulosic biomass and residues, including wood chips, sawdust and wheat straw, into ethanol. This can subsequently be upgraded into SAF using an alcohol-to-jet process, as well as being used to produce renewable diesel.

The process also produces biochar as a co-product. Nova Pangaea says the carbon stored in the biochar enables its overall process to achieve net-negative emissions, removing more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than it releases.

The technology is being developed at a time when policymakers are seeking to increase SAF production while reducing the industry’s dependence on fuels derived from waste oils and fats.

The UK’s SAF Mandate requires 3.6% of jet fuel supplied in 2026 to come from sustainable sources, increasing to 10% in 2030 and 22% in 2040.1 The mandate also progressively restricts the amount that can be met using hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), currently the principal commercial SAF production route, in an effort to encourage more advanced fuels using alternative feedstocks.2

Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird, which aims to establish a UK supply chain converting locally sourced waste biomass into ethanol before upgrading it to SAF.

Under the project, Nova Pangaea plans to construct four UK facilities producing bioethanol from waste biomass.

Commercial scale

The latest trials come as Nova Pangaea prepares to seek further investment to progress its first commercial-scale plant. The company has raised more than £21 million to date from investors including International Airlines Group, PXN Ventures and Mercia Ventures, alongside UK government funding through the Advanced Fuels Fund.

Stewart Stewart, CEO of Nova Pangaea, said: “The latest trials have validated our technology and should further underpin the confidence of investors on our journey towards building our first commercial plant.

“The SAF industry is currently at a critical point. Demand is increasing and supply chain shocks such as in the Middle East show the need to find an alternative to fossil fuels, yet aviation is currently reliant on SAF from a single feedstock, which will not be enough to meet growing SAF demand.

“Nova Pangaea’s tried and tested technology offers a genuine alternative. By tapping into the plentiful supplies of waste biomass, we can boost SAF production – enhancing our energy security and building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and revenues while reducing fossil fuel emissions.”

The UK government has acknowledged the limitations of relying heavily on HEFA fuels, which depend on constrained supplies of oils and fats. Its SAF policy is intended to encourage diversification into advanced production pathways and feedstocks capable of contributing a greater share as mandated SAF volumes increase.3

text: A California startup says it has completed an end-to-end pilot that converted raw dairy-farm biogas into sustainable aviation fuel. Circularity Fuels operated the system for six months using biogas supplied directly by a manure digester at a California dairy farm. The incoming gas contained approximately 65% methane and 35% carbon dioxide. The company’s process begins with an electrified reactor called Ouro, which converts the biogas into synthesis gas—a mixture containing carbon monoxide and hydrogen. A second unit, called Aion, then uses Fischer–Tropsch synthesis to turn that gas into a liquid fuel mixture. Circularity says the resulting jet fuel met the requirements of ASTM D7566 Annex A1, the approved pathway covering Fischer–Tropsch synthetic paraffinic kerosene. Fuel produced through this pathway can be blended with conventional Jet A at concentrations of up to 50%. During the pilot, the Ouro reactor reportedly converted more than 98% of the methane and over 90% of the carbon dioxide in a single step. These performance figures and the project’s “world-first” description come from Circularity Fuels. This was a pilot rather than a commercial fuel-production facility. The company is now building a demonstration system targeting approximately 10 gallons per day. Circularity’s published roadmap calls for its first commercial plant to produce one million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually, with operations targeted for early 2029.

text:
Sustainability investment is increasingly moving beyond symbolic corporate pledges, becoming a decisive factor in infrastructure development, financing strategies, and resource management across key industries. Innovations in sustainable aviation fuel, renewable energy integration for data centers, advanced water management techniques, and the emergence of natural capital markets illustrate how both private and public sectors are responding to intensifying environmental challenges.

This transformation is visible across a broad geographic spectrum, from Latin America and the United States to Southeast Asia, where businesses now regard emissions reduction, energy security, water availability, and ecosystem valuation as integral commercial priorities rather than peripheral environmental concerns. In regions such as Africa, where infrastructure gaps and limited access to climate finance persist, these global trends offer valuable insights into embedding sustainability within investment frameworks.

Aviation: From Pledges to Concrete Action

The aviation industry, long recognized as one of the most difficult sectors to decarbonize due to the limitations of battery technology and direct electrification for long-haul flights, is beginning to implement tangible sustainability measures. A notable development is the framework agreement between Syzygy Plasmonics and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to explore sustainable aviation fuel projects across Latin America. Syzygy’s innovative light-driven technology, combined with the IFC’s role as a development finance institution, highlights the importance of bridging the gap between pilot technologies and commercially viable, bankable projects.

Globally, airlines and manufacturers are adopting diverse strategies to reduce their environmental impact. Initiatives such as the United Kingdom’s ‘Operation Blue Skies’ and electric air service trials in Norway and Sweden exemplify proactive efforts to advance sustainable aviation. Collaborations between major players like Airbus and Air Canada on sustainable aviation fuel projects further demonstrate industry commitment. Meanwhile, companies such as Bombardier are enhancing transparency by publicly disclosing their full environmental footprints. For emerging markets, particularly in Africa where aviation demand is expected to grow, success will hinge on developing the necessary infrastructure, securing reliable electricity supplies, establishing feedstock supply chains, implementing certification systems, and attracting long-term capital investment.

AI and Data Centers: Emerging Sustainability Pressures

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) is introducing new sustainability challenges, especially concerning the energy and water demands of data centers. ENGIE’s recent 48-megawatt solar power purchase agreement with data center operator QTS in Texas exemplifies how operators are increasingly relying on long-term renewable energy contracts to address rising electricity consumption and associated emissions. As AI drives demand for high-performance computing, data centers face growing pressure from investors and customers alike to minimize their environmental footprint.

However, renewable energy procurement addresses only part of the sustainability equation. Data centers also require substantial water resources for cooling, which can place significant strain on local utilities. Companies such as Gradiant are expanding their focus on water management solutions tailored to data centers and semiconductor manufacturing facilities, reflecting heightened concerns about the capacity of communities to support expanding digital infrastructure in terms of both energy and water availability.

Investment Challenges and Market Uncertainty

The transition from corporate sustainability pledges to substantial infrastructure investment entails significant financial commitments and inherent risks. Fitch Ratings has cautioned about the potential for a market correction in the AI sector, noting that uncertainties surrounding AI’s long-term revenue prospects could complicate investment decisions. Market responses are likely to be uneven, with some sectors advancing rapidly while others adopt a more cautious approach.

As sustainability increasingly becomes a core element of commercial strategy, the dynamic interplay between technological innovation, financing mechanisms, and regulatory frameworks will be critical in determining how effectively industries can achieve environmental objectives while managing economic risks. This evolving landscape underscores the imperative for coordinated action among corporations, investors, and governments to ensure that sustainability commitments are translated into practical, scalable solutions.

text:
O caminho do mundo para um processo de descarbonização tem no etanol um ativo fundamental para esse objetivo de segurança climática e sustentável. O etanol, obtido por meio da fermentação de açúcares de origem vegetal como a cana-de-açúcar e o milho, é fundamental por ser uma alternativa limpa aos combustíveis fósseis. Com uso já consolidado nos veículos terrestres por meio de misturas nas gasolinas, o biocombustível tem um alto potencial nos transportes marítimo e aéreo.

No Brasil, essa expansão beneficia setores estratégicos como o sucroenergético, com a abertura de novas rotas comerciais e fortalecimento de regiões como o Nordeste. De acordo com o presidente do Sindicato da Indústria do Açúcar e do Álcool no Estado de Pernambuco (Sindaçúcar-PE) e presidente-executivo da NovaBio, Renato Cunha, a cana-de-açúcar é uma matéria-prima aproveitada em diferentes processos industriais.

“Da cana, praticamente tudo pode ser utilizado. O bagaço, por exemplo, é uma fibra resultante da moagem que serve como fonte de energia limpa para movimentar as usinas, sem necessidade de energia externa para grande parte da operação industrial e da geração de bioeletricidade”, explica.

“Da cana, praticamente tudo pode ser utilizado", diz Renato Cunha Foto: Paullo Allmeida/Folha de Pernabuco

Versatilidade

A cana permite a produção de açúcar, bioeletricidade, melaço e etanol. “No processo de fabricação do açúcar é gerado o melaço, um produto derivado da cana que pode ser destinado à alimentação animal, ao uso em tecnologias na área de saúde, bem como em rotas álcoolquímicas e na produção carburante de etanol”, afirma Cunha.

Ainda segundo o gestor, no Brasil, de 51% a 54% do volume da cana-de-açúcar processada é destinada ao etanol, enquanto a parcela restante é voltada para a produção de açúcar.

O presidente da Associação da Indústria da Bioenergia e do Açúcar de Minas Gerais (SIAMIG Bioenergia) e da Bioenergia Brasil, Mário Campos, elenca três pontos como os pilares da construção da demanda por etanol no curto e médio prazo: o mercado doméstico, com o aumento da participação do etanol na matriz de transportes leves, misturas de etanol em gasolina pelo mundo e mercado marítimo.

“Para longo prazo, teríamos o SAF (Combustível Sustentável de Aviação) como alternativa e também as estruturas de termelétricas, ou seja, geração de energia elétrica utilizando estruturas de etanol”, reitera Mário Campos.

Marítimo

Na área marítima, o avanço do etanol está ligado às metas estabelecidas pela International Maritime Organization (IMO). “A organização tem como objetivo alcançar o net zero, ou seja, emissões líquidas zero, até 2050. A expectativa é de que o etanol ganhe aprovações para uso em maior escala no setor marítimo. Os testes já começaram, inicialmente com misturas de 10% aos combustíveis convencionais”, destaca Renato Cunha.

O presidente da Datagro, Plínio Nastari, enfatiza o tamanho do potencial do etanol no setor marítimo. Segundo ele, atualmente toda a produção global de etanol (considerando combustível e outros usos industriais) é de aproximadamente 100 milhões de toneladas, o que equivale a 125 bilhões de litros. “O consumo do etanol no transporte marítimo tem um potencial de até 225 milhões de toneladas. É um consumo superlativo”, afirma.

Segundo Nastari, consumo do etanol no transporte marítimo tem um potencial de até 225 milhões de toneladas Foto: Divulgação

Ainda de acordo com Nastari, o Nordeste está em uma posição geográfica importante e deve se tornar um relevante e eficiente hub de abastecimento de rotas marítimas.

“Rotas que saiam da América do Norte, que vão contornar o Cabo da Boa Esperança ou que caminhe para outras rotas, até para a Europa, poderão ter o abastecimento com combustível etanol certificado de baixa emissão no Nordeste. A diversificação do uso de etanol é muito importante e superestratégica para o Nordeste”, revela.

Para Renato Cunha, os portos nordestinos terão papel estratégico no avanço das exportações de biocombustíveis como o etanol.

“Nos próximos anos, até 2050, não seremos apenas importadores de produtos, mas também exportadores. Os portos terão uma vocação mais ampla no Nordeste em função da proximidade logística com os centros de produção e da possibilidade de fazer abastecimentos mais contínuos através das plataformas de exportação que já existem na região.”

Segundo ele, a eficiência logística dos portos da região deve fortalecer o comércio exterior nordestino e impulsionar as exportações nos próximos anos.

“Agora, o comércio vai ter uma mão dupla em função dos portos eficientes das capitais do Nordeste, como Suape, Recife, Maceió, Natal, Cabedelo, Itaqui, no Maranhão, Pecém e Mucuripe, entre outros. Todos esses portos estarão vivendo um grande momento, não só para receber cargas, mas também para exportá-las.”

Suape

O Complexo Industrial Portuário de Suape, localizado no Litoral Sul de Pernambuco, está na vanguarda da transição energética. Segundo o diretor-presidente do porto, Armando Monteiro Bisneto, o atracadouro tem todas as condições para ser um polo de distribuição e de fomento do etanol para o uso como combustível marítimo.

“O Porto de Suape vem se preparando de algumas formas. Uma delas é que a gente tem a maior tancagem estática dentro de um porto organizado no Brasil. Cerca de 65% do movimento de Suape é de granéis líquidos, ou seja, de combustíveis. Então, Suape tem toda a condição de estocar e fornecer o etanol para os seus dois terminais de contêineres. Suape é o único porto do Norte/Nordeste que tem dois terminais de contêineres agora.”

O gestor aponta que, apesar do etanol existir desde a criação do Programa Nacional do Álcool (Proálcool) em 1975, o biocombustível se mantém cada vez mais atual.

“O etanol vai servir para criar os corredores verdes entre os portos, abastecendo navios, vai ser usado para termelétricas e a cana-de-açúcar tem essa versatilidade. A biomassa da cana ainda pode ser utilizada para capturar o CO2 biogênico para fabricação de combustíveis sintéticos.”

Em maio deste ano, foi anunciada a conclusão da implantação da primeira termelétrica do mundo movida a etanol no Porto de Suape. Denominado de Projeto Etanol, a iniciativa foi desenvolvida pela Suape Energia, em parceria com a multinacional finlandesa Wärtsilä. A proposta da térmica é utilizar o etanol como combustível na geração de energia elétrica em larga escala.

Segundo o diretor-técnico da Suape Energia, José Faustino da Costa Cândido, o objetivo do projeto é mostrar para o fabricante de máquina e para o fornecedor de combustível que é viável ter uma planta de etanol para compor a matriz energética brasileira e dar sustentação às fontes solar e eólica.

José Faustino da Costa Cândido, diretor-técnico da Suape Energia Foto: Suape Energia/Divulgação

“É o primeiro motor em larga escala. Estou falando de 4 MW que vai ser testado na nossa usina aqui em Pernambuco, para que mostremos ao mercado que é eficiente, não só na parte de performance, mas também na parte econômico-financeira. Você combina a parte econômico-financeira com a viabilidade tecnológica, de performance, e de equipamento, com a história da transição da matriz energética. E você tem uma termelétrica agora funcionando com um combustível renovável.”

Setor aéreo

No transporte aéreo, o etanol pode ser utilizado para produzir o Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), ou Combustível Sustentável de Aviação. O biocombustível surge como uma alternativa ao Querosene de Aviação (QAV), derivado do petróleo. Para Renato Cunha, no entanto, o processo de descarbonização da aviação deve avançar, de início, de forma mais branda, do que no setor marítimo.

“O etanol para aviação tem um processo de beneficiamento industrial (espécie de quebra de moléculas) para o uso e depende futuramente da competitividade de preços. O consumidor, que é o usuário do avião, à primeira vista, terá que despender um preço acrescido de um incentivo, pelo menos na fase inicial do BIOQAV (Bioquerosene de Aviação), porque poderá ter custos que serão melhor equalizados em um segundo momento, na fase de transição”, explica.

Plínio Nastari reitera que, para utilizar o etanol na produção de SAF, é necessário um alto investimento. “São cerca de 1,2 a 1,5 dólar por litro de etanol a ser convertido em SAF. A produção de SAF exige investimentos vultosos. Porém, essa rota também vai acontecer, porque existe um mandato de descarbonização no transporte aéreo que precisa ser cumprido”, destaca.

Produção

A estimativa de produção na safra 2026/2027, que já está em andamento, é de aproximadamente 42 bilhões de litros de etanol. Do volume, cerca de 29 bilhões devem ser oriundos da cana e 12,7 bilhões do milho. A quantidade é utilizada em veículos de transportes e cargas, como tratores e caminhões, e na área marítima, que já está em fase de testes.

“São utilizados 10% de etanol ou até níveis maiores de mistura em navios, junto com o combustível que é o bunker marítimo. Misturando essa porcentagem, são 50 bilhões de litros, um mercado maior do que a própria produção brasileira hoje”, reitera Renato Cunha.

Na área veicular, são utilizados, no Brasil, 32% (E32) de etanol anidro misturado à gasolina. “Os dois maiores mercados (em termos de produção) são Estados Unidos e Brasil. Os Estados Unidos produzem em torno de 60 bilhões de litros”, informa o presidente do Sindaçúcar-PE.

Apesar do potencial de crescimento do biocombustível, o presidente da Associação da Indústria da Bioenergia e do Açúcar de Minas Gerais (SIAMIG Bioenergia) e da Bioenergia Brasil, Mário Campos, alerta que a expansão da produção precisa ocorrer de forma equilibrada para acompanhar o aumento da demanda.

“O que vimos nos últimos anos em termos de aumento da produção de etanol a partir de grãos, e na velocidade desse crescimento, demonstrou que temos forte capacidade de ampliar a escala produtiva. No sistema da cana, também há grandes possibilidades. O grande desafio é ajustar o equilíbrio entre oferta e demanda, porque esses sistemas produtivos são, em alguns casos, verticalizados. Algumas estruturas exigem alto investimento e, obviamente, esse capital e essas estruturas precisam ser bem remuneradas”, explica.

Regulamentação

Na avaliação de Renato Cunha, 2025 e 2026 foram fundamentais para o setor de etanol devido à aprovação de marcos regulatórios no Brasil.

A Lei do Combustível do Futuro, e programas como o de Aceleração da Transição Energética (Paten) e de Mobilidade Verde e Inovação (Mover), são relevantes para impulsionar o setor no País. “Houve também a COP30, em Belém, onde o etanol marcou presença e se diferenciou”, menciona.

Referência

O Brasil é protagonista na produção de energias renováveis e é referência na transição energética. No País, quase metade da energia disponibilizada (49,5%) vem de fontes renováveis, marcada pelo aumento da oferta interna de eólica e solar, associado à queda de energia hidráulica.

A maior parte (50,5%), no entanto, ainda é produzida a partir de recursos fósseis, com o crescimento do gás natural, segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional 2026, ano-base 2025, divulgado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Em 2024, o percentual de renováveis era de 50%.

Entre as renováveis destacam-se a biomassa da cana que inclui a produção de etanol (15,8%), a hidráulica (10,7%), e a lenha e o carvão vegetal (8,3%).

O licor preto e outras renováveis representam 8,9%, a eólica 3,1% e a solar, 2,7%. No caso das não renováveis, os maiores percentuais estão com o petróleo e seus derivados (33,7%), o gás natural (10,4%) e o carvão mineral (4,3%).

Mário Campos, presidente da SIAMIG Bioenergia e Bioenergia Brasil Foto: SIAMIG Bioenergia/Divulgação

“A energia que hoje é produzida a partir da cana-de-açúcar tem uma posição de destaque, não só por ofertar um produto de baixa emissão, mas também por trazer uma estrutura que emprega muitos brasileiros, gerando emprego e renda em diversas localidades e regiões produtivas do Brasil”, pontua Mário Campos.

Em um cenário diferente da realidade brasileira, as fontes fósseis representam 85,4% da geração na matriz energética mundial. Já as fontes renováveis respondem pelos 14,5% restantes, de acordo com a Agência Internacional de Energia (cuja sigla em inglês é IEA) de 2025, ano-base 2023.

title: Want to get a united East Africa, economically? Try the sugarcane - The EastAfrican
description:
We are paying for the mirage of economic integration under the East African Community that has been under re-construction for a quarter of a century.
That is the scandal of East African aviation in three Ps: Paperwork, Pettiness, Pride, not Distance, Demand nor Dignity.
Now, there are two things the region keeps talking about separately — cheap flights and clean fuel — which are actually the same fight.
That has set off a scramble everywhere for something to make clean fuel.
And East Africa, without quite noticing, is sitting on a very good answer: sugarcane.
text:
As I advance in years and can no longer be immediately productive after being battered by a road trip of 12 to 24 hours, I start asking why a 45-minute hop from Entebbe to Nairobi should cost $400 in economy class, same as Entebbe to Dubai, which is ten times longer. So what exactly are we paying for?

We are paying for the mirage of economic integration under the East African Community that has been under re-construction for a quarter of a century. Landing fees here, navigation charges there, VAT on top, airport tax on top of that top as each border adds its own little toll booth in the sky. That is the scandal of East African aviation in three Ps: Paperwork, Pettiness, Pride, not Distance, Demand nor Dignity.

Now, there are two things the region keeps talking about separately — cheap flights and clean fuel — which are actually the same fight. You cannot win one without the other, and if our governments finally worked that out, they could kill two birds with one very well-fuelled stone.

Here’s the logic: The whole world is being pushed to put “green” fuel in its jets — Sustainable Aviation Fuel business, SAF in short. Europe made it the law; every plane leaving a European airport must carry a rising share of SAF, no arguments. That has set off a scramble everywhere for something to make clean fuel. And East Africa, without quite noticing, is sitting on a very good answer: sugarcane.

South African farmers found this out — that cane run through a fermentation process into ethanol and then upgraded a step further, makes certifiable, lawful jet fuel — approved by the international standards body since 2018. In Uganda, the populous Basoga community embraced a presidential candidate they knew next to nothing about in 2021 because sugarcane prices had hit rock bottom. In SA, cane farmers squeezed by falling sugar prices turned to research, and found clean jet fuel! The beautiful prospect for East Africa is that you don’t have to touch the sugar business — just use the molasses — the leftover sludge our millers currently sell off cheap. Simply stop wasting what the millers frown at.

But, and this is what our petty side hates to hear, no single EAC country can build this alone. A proper fuel refinery is not a village project. It needs hundreds of millions of dollars and a guaranteed river of cane feeding it all year-round, more than Uganda’s, Tanzania’s or Kenya’s fields could promise on their own. Put the whole bloc’s cane belts together, and you have enough raw material to interest serious investors. Build the thing once, jointly, at Kisumu, Mwanza or Entebbe on our Mother Lake Victoria, and you supply every airport in the region from one plant. Exactly what Europe does across 27 countries with one shared rulebook.

Which brings me back to my opening complaint. Why bother building a regional fuel industry if the flights it is meant to power still cost $400 for 45 minutes? Nobody invests hundreds of millions in fuel nobody can afford to fly on. The two projects need each other. Cheap, borderless flights create the demand that makes a joint SAF plant worth building. A joint SAF plant gives our governments a real, shared economic reason — beyond the usual summit speeches — to finally agree on one set of skies. You cannot sell one without the other, and frankly, we have been trying to sell one without the other for twenty-five years and getting nowhere.

And it is not only about passengers grumbling over ticket prices, either — though heaven knows we have earned the right to grumble. Cheaper, more frequent flights mean our flowers, our fish, our avocados and our medicines can actually move by air instead of rotting in a customs queue or crawling along the highway. That is money in a farmer’s pocket, not just comfort for a tourist.

The cane is already growing in the ground, doing nothing much for anyone but the miller. The only thing missing is eight governments willing to admit they are, in fact, one economy — and act like it, for once.

title: The Banking Problem in African Skies - Aviation Metric
description:
African airlines are expected to generate only about $200 million in net profit in 2026, a margin of about 1%, despite approximately 6% demand growth.
More recently, the outlook has deteriorated further under higher fuel prices and geopolitical disruption, with IATA forecasting an even thinner 2026 margin for African airlines.
African airlines frequently face the additional burden of high country risk, currency volatility, limited access to foreign exchange and relatively weak balance sheets.
Money cannot solve every African aviation problem.
Only about 19% of intra-African routes have direct flights, while African airlines continue to face high costs and limited profitability.
text:
There are industries in which money follows opportunity. Aviation is one of them. There are also industries in which the absence of appropriate financing prevents the opportunity from ever becoming a reality. African aviation belongs increasingly to the second category.

The continent has people who want to travel, businesses that need to move, airports that want to expand, airlines that want to acquire aircraft, cargo operators that need equipment, maintenance companies that need facilities and governments that want connectivity.

What is often missing is not the demand, the ambition or even the resources. It is patient, specialised and appropriately structured capital.

That is why I propose that Africa should seriously consider establishing a Bank of Aviation. Let us be clear: what is needed is not another commercial bank with an aviation desk.

Not another government intervention fund that appears when an airline is already in distress. And certainly not a financial institution created to keep chronically inefficient airlines alive.

A Bank of Aviation would be a more purposeful initiative: a specialised financial institution dedicated to financing the infrastructure, equipment, enterprises and ecosystems required to build a competitive African aviation industry. Readers of these pages will know it is not a position, but the case is stronger now than it has ever been.

The first mistake when discussing aviation finance is to treat aviation as merely another commercial activity. Let me repeat what I keep saying at every turn: Aviation is infrastructure.

Aviation connects markets, people, capital, skills, tourism, trade and investment. IATA has made this case precisely, describing aviation as economic infrastructure for Africa and calling on governments to treat it as a strategic enabler of development. Yet the financial architecture supporting African aviation remains remarkably weak.

African airlines are expected to generate only about $200 million in net profit in 2026, a margin of about 1%, despite approximately 6% demand growth.

African carriers remain the least profitable regional airline group because of high fuel costs, fragmented markets, older fleets, high taxes and charges, and other structural disadvantages.

More recently, the outlook has deteriorated further under higher fuel prices and geopolitical disruption, with IATA forecasting an even thinner 2026 margin for African airlines. This is not simply an airline profitability problem. It is a capital problem.

You cannot operate an airline without aircraft. That sounds obvious, but the financing implications are profound. An aircraft is an extraordinarily expensive asset, purchased in a currency that is usually stronger than the one in which the airline earns much of its revenue.

Aircraft are financed through a mix of equity, debt, leasing and manufacturer arrangements. The financial sophistication required to structure these transactions is substantial.

African airlines frequently face the additional burden of high country risk, currency volatility, limited access to foreign exchange and relatively weak balance sheets.

Research has identified limited financial capacity and access to capital as constraints on fleet expansion and network development in Africa.

We must include aircraft and spare parts shortages, small average fleet sizes, and foreign-currency constraints as factors limiting growth.

The African airline is trapped in an uncomfortable cycle. It needs more aircraft to expand. It needs expansion to improve connectivity and economies of scale.

But it needs stronger finances to obtain the aircraft. And it needs the aircraft and stronger networks to improve those finances. That is precisely the sort of cycle specialised finance is designed to break.

One might ask: why create another bank? Commercial banks already finance businesses. Aircraft lessors already exist. Development banks already provide infrastructure finance. Governments already have intervention funds. All true, but aviation finance is not ordinary corporate lending.

An aviation lender must understand aircraft values, residual values, leases, maintenance reserves, engine cycles, route economics, traffic rights, airport concessions, aviation insurance, foreign-exchange exposure, aircraft registration, repossession risks and international aviation law.

To do business with aviation, you must understand that a Boeing 737 is not simply an expensive machine. It is a mobile financial asset whose value depends on its age, configuration, maintenance status, market demand and ability to operate in particular jurisdictions.

The lender or investor must understand the difference between financing an airline and financing an airport. It must understand why a maintenance, repair, and overhaul facility may be more strategically valuable to a region than to another airline. It must understand cargo. It must understand the value of training. It must understand aviation technology.

Aviation needs bankers who understand aviation, and aviation professionals who understand finance. The place to bring them together will be in an aviation bank.

The next logical and legitimate question is what this bank will finance. Let us start by clarifying that a properly conceived Bank of Aviation should not be an airline bailout institution. Its mandate should cover the wider aviation ecosystem.

The African Bank of Aviation will provide long-term financing and leasing support for qualifying airlines seeking to acquire new or used aircraft.

It will also finance the replacement of inefficient and ageing aircraft, fund airports, terminals, hangars, cargo facilities, navigation infrastructure and associated projects, and finance MRO facilities so that African airlines do not have to send aircraft thousands of kilometres away for maintenance that could be performed competitively within the continent.

It will fund aviation academies, simulators and professional training infrastructure, support digital ticketing, payments, revenue management, safety systems, air-traffic technologies and other aviation technology companies, finance warehouses, cold-chain facilities, cargo terminals and specialised logistics infrastructure, and finance renewable-energy systems, efficiency improvements, sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure and other transition investments.

The objective would be to create a financial ecosystem for aviation, rather than merely finding money for airlines. The Bank should finance viability, not failure, and this distinction is essential. Africa has had enough experiences in which public money is used to postpone rather than solve structural problems.

An African Bank of Aviation should therefore apply strict commercial and developmental criteria. It should ask: Is the project viable? Is the management competent?

Is the route commercially defensible? Is the governance credible? Is the financing structure sustainable? What is the security? What is the exit? And perhaps most importantly: Does this investment increase the productive capacity of African aviation?

The prediction is straightforward. A bank that lends simply because an airline is politically important will eventually become a warehouse for bad debt. A bank that finances viable aviation assets and businesses can become an engine of transformation.

Allow me to be the first to say that the idea is not as radical as it sounds. The aviation industry already has specialised financial infrastructure.

IATA’s financial settlement systems processed more than $471 billion in 2024, facilitating transactions among airlines, travel agents, freight forwarders and other aviation stakeholders.

In 2025, IATA reports that its financial settlement systems processed $492.4 billion. These figures are important. They demonstrate that aviation is already a financial ecosystem of extraordinary scale.

The question is why Africa should remain primarily a consumer of global aviation finance rather than developing stronger institutions capable of mobilising and structuring capital for its own aviation development.

A Bank of Aviation could work alongside institutions such as IATA, AFRAA, African development finance institutions, commercial banks, aircraft manufacturers, leasing companies and institutional investors. It would not replace them. Rather, it would connect them.

This concept might be more compelling as a multinational African aviation finance entity rather than a traditional bank created by a single government.

Let us imagine together a structure that includes African governments, development finance institutions, sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, commercial banks, airlines, airports, institutional investors, aircraft manufacturers, leasing companies, and insurance institutions.

The bank could be capitalised through a combination of paid-in capital, guarantees, institutional investment and carefully structured bonds.

Its balance sheet could then support projects that ordinary commercial banks might regard as too specialised or too long-term.

This is precisely where development finance can make a difference: not by replacing the market, but by enabling commercially viable investments where risk, tenor, or information asymmetry otherwise prevents capital from entering.

A governance question must not be avoided from the outset. If airlines alone control the bank, there will be a temptation to prioritise airline financing.

That would be too narrow. The aviation ecosystem is much larger. The shareholders should include institutions with long-term capital and a development perspective, while the governance structure should include strong professional representation from aviation, finance, risk management, law and infrastructure.

Lending policies should be strict and well-regulated, including independent credit committees, transparent procurement, audited accounts, and professional risk management. No borrower should be exempt from these standards, even if they bear a national flag.

An airline failing to meet the bank’s commercial and governance criteria should not qualify for funding merely because it represents a nation’s symbol. The bank’s goal is to support the growth of African aviation, not to shield poorly managed airlines from accountability.

This proposal should not be misunderstood. Money cannot solve every African aviation problem. The continent still needs regulatory reform, open markets, better infrastructure, lower taxes and charges, improved safety systems, stronger institutions and more seamless connectivity.

Only about 19% of intra-African routes have direct flights, while African airlines continue to face high costs and limited profitability. There is also the problem of blocked airline funds. IATA reported that African countries accounted for the largest share of globally blocked airline revenues, with US$774 million blocked in Africa as of the end of March 2026.

A bank cannot make a government honour its currency obligations. It cannot liberalise air services agreements.

It cannot remove visa restrictions. It cannot turn an incompetent regulator into a competent one. A bank can, however, do something governments often struggle with, namely provide disciplined, specialised and patient capital. And capital matters.

Let us be clear. The deeper issue is not whether Africa needs another bank. Africa has banks. Africa has development finance institutions. Africa has pension funds. Africa has sovereign funds. Africa has wealthy individuals. Africa has international investors.

The question is whether these pools of capital are properly connected to aviation opportunities. Too often, aviation is discussed as an industry that consumes capital. We should begin discussing it as an industry that creates economic infrastructure and multiplies capital.

A new airport can create a logistics ecosystem. A cargo terminal can expand export capacity. An MRO facility can retain foreign exchange. A training academy can create skilled employment. A fleet expansion can improve connectivity.

Connectivity can boost tourism. Tourism can create businesses. Businesses create jobs. Jobs create incomes. And incomes create demand. That is how infrastructure becomes development. This, ultimately, is the case for a Bank of Aviation.

The purpose should not be simply to help African airlines buy more aircraft. Its purpose should be to help Africa build an aviation ecosystem capable of financing, expanding, and competing globally.

It should finance aircraft, yes, but also engines, hangars, training, technology, cargo, airports, maintenance, renewable energy, logistics, start-ups, infrastructure, and the human capital that holds all of these together.

The aim should be to create a virtuous cycle: improved finance leads to better assets, which enhance connectivity, reduce costs, strengthen businesses, attract more investment, and further improve connectivity.

Those who continue to describe Africa’s aviation challenge as a demand shortage are mistaken. Africa’s aviation challenge is increasingly a shortage of capacity, connectivity and capital. The first two require policy, while the third requires institutions. It is time for Africa to build one.

Let us start with the African Aviation Bank, not to rescue the aviation industry from its past, but to finance the aviation industry Africa will need for its future.

*Anthony Kila, the author of “Strategy Systems and Power in Flight: Lessons in Strategy, Leadership and Institution Building from Aviation”, is a Jean Monnet Professor of Strategy and Development at the Commonwealth Institute of Advanced and Professional Studies (CIAPS). He also serves as Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of the Governing Council of the Michael and Cecilia Ibru University (MCIU). He is the founding Chairman of Sabre Africa Travel Network.

title: 荷兰首座专用SAF工厂开建，计划2028年投产 - 搜狐
description:
Scheduled to become operational in 2028, the facility is expected to produce around 100,000 tonnes of SAF annually using low-quality feedstocks, including used cooking oil and residual fats and greases.
The plant will use the Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) pathway to produce SAF with significantly lower lifecycle emissions than conventional jet fuel, while also generating renewable co-products such as propane, butane and naphtha.

Market Challenges & Opportunities

Challenges

The Sustainable Aviation Fuel Market faces several notable challenges. The SAF cost premium over conventional jet fuel—currently trading at 2–4 times the price—represents the most significant restraint, with HEFA-based SAF carrying a premium of USD 1,500–3,000 per metric ton depending on pathway and feedstock [20]. BloombergNEF projects the premium will narrow to 1.5–2x by 2030 as production scales, but near-term margin compression remains a drag on adoption velocity [21].

Feedstock availability and competition with road biofuels pose another constraint, with UCO facing intense competition from renewable diesel producers serving road transport mandates [13][22]. Blend wall limitations under current ASTM standards—which approve SAF blending at up to 50% by volume—restrict total displacement potential even at airports with abundant supply [14]. Infrastructure gaps at secondary and regional airports, and certification lead times for novel pathways (typically 5–7 years from lab demonstration to commercial approval), further challenge market growth.

Significant opportunities exist in the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Market. Emerging market SAF adoption through CORSIA compliance creates greenfield opportunities for technology licensors and feedstock aggregators in developing nations [11][24]. Book-and-claim SAF accounting and digital certification platforms unlock demand from airlines operating at airports without SAF supply infrastructure, potentially adding 15–20% incremental demand above physical supply constraints [25]. Corporate travel SAF programs and Scope 3 reporting frameworks (CDP, TCFD, CSRD) create a parallel demand channel independent of airline procurement, with companies like Microsoft signing multi-year SAF procurement deals exceeding USD 50 million [4].

title: Kenya Airways Orders Major Contract Review as Rising Fuel Cost Surge Hits Nairobi Operations
description:
Kamal told journalists in Nairobi that Kenya Airways was reviewing its contracts and looking for opportunities to save money.
Nairobi Hub Makes Fleet Recovery Particularly Important Kenya Airways occupies an important position within African aviation.
Previous Financial Recovery Faces Another Test The cost pressure comes after a turbulent financial period for Kenya Airways.
Kenya Airways Situation Reflects Wider African Aviation Pressures The problems facing Kenya Airways have implications beyond Kenya.
Second Half of 2026 Becomes Critical for Kenya Airways Kenya Airways now faces a demanding balancing act.
text:
Kenya Airways is intensifying efforts to control its expenses after a sharp rise in fuel costs added another challenge to the airline’s financial recovery.

The Kenyan flag carrier says its fuel costs increased by 72% during the first half of 2026, with management linking the increase to the continuing conflict in the Middle East and its effect on energy markets. Fuel now represents as much as 50% of the airline’s total costs, making expenditure control an urgent priority.

Acting Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer George Kamal has consequently revealed that Kenya Airways is examining its contracts as it searches for savings across the business.

The development comes at a particularly important moment for the airline. Passenger demand remains strong, but limited aircraft availability and global supply-chain problems are restricting its ability to take full advantage of that demand.

Kenya Airways Turns to Cost Cutting After Fuel Shock

The scale of the fuel increase has forced management to look closely at expenses throughout the airline.

Kamal told journalists in Nairobi that Kenya Airways was reviewing its contracts and looking for opportunities to save money.

The pressure is particularly significant because the airline operates with narrow margins. Kamal said Kenya Airways makes only around $1.50 profit per seat, demonstrating why even relatively small cost savings can become important when multiplied across thousands of flights and passengers.

Fuel represents one of the largest expenses faced by commercial airlines.

When energy prices rise rapidly, airlines cannot simply stop purchasing fuel. They must instead find efficiencies elsewhere, manage capacity carefully or increase the revenue generated from their operations.

For Kenya Airways, the latest increase has made that balancing act considerably harder.

Middle East Crisis Reaches African Aviation

The financial impact demonstrates how events far beyond East Africa can quickly affect African airlines.

The conflict in the Middle East has disrupted global energy markets and contributed to higher fuel expenditure. Aviation is particularly exposed because aircraft consume large amounts of jet fuel and international airlines operate across complex supply chains.

Kenya Airways says the impact has not been limited to fuel.

The airline is also experiencing delays involving aircraft spare parts and maintenance, while wider inflation is adding to operating pressure.

These problems illustrate the interconnected nature of modern aviation. A disruption affecting manufacturers, logistics providers or international transportation networks can eventually leave aircraft unavailable thousands of kilometres away.

Aircraft Shortages Restrict Kenya Airways Capacity

Fleet availability is becoming another critical concern.

Kenya Airways has a fleet of around 40 aircraft, meaning prolonged maintenance or delayed aircraft deliveries can have a substantial effect on its ability to provide capacity.

Kamal said global aircraft supply problems affect many airlines, but Kenya Airways’ relatively small fleet leaves it particularly exposed.

The carrier is waiting for two Boeing 737 aircraft. Two other aircraft expected earlier in the year were rejected after failing inspection tests.

That situation creates a difficult commercial problem because Kenya Airways says passenger demand is strong.

According to Kamal, routes where the airline deploys aircraft are operating with strong demand, increasing the urgency of bringing additional capacity into the network.

Nairobi Hub Makes Fleet Recovery Particularly Important

Kenya Airways occupies an important position within African aviation.

Its Nairobi hub provides connections between numerous African destinations while also linking passengers with markets outside the continent.

Aircraft shortages can therefore have consequences extending beyond passengers beginning or ending their journeys in Kenya.

Connecting travellers rely on coordinated schedules to move through Nairobi towards other destinations. Tour operators also depend on sufficient air capacity when packaging safaris, beach holidays and multi-country East African itineraries.

Improving fleet availability would give Kenya Airways greater flexibility to respond to demand and protect the connectivity provided through Nairobi.

Will Kenya Airways Airfares Increase?

The sharp increase in fuel expenditure inevitably raises questions about ticket prices.

However, passengers should not assume that a 72% increase in fuel costs will automatically produce a similar increase in fares.

Kenya Airways has not announced a general fare increase directly matching the fuel-cost surge.

Airfares are determined by several factors, including passenger demand, available seats, competition, seasonality, route performance and booking timing.

Nevertheless, sustained cost pressure can affect airline pricing decisions over time.

For travellers and tourism businesses, monitoring fares and booking conditions will therefore remain important during the remainder of 2026.

Strong Demand Creates an Unusual Challenge

One of the most striking elements of Kenya Airways’ current position is the contrast between demand and capacity.

The airline is not describing a shortage of passengers. Instead, it needs additional aircraft to capture existing demand more effectively.

That changes the nature of the challenge.

When an airline has weak demand, reducing capacity can help limit losses. But when demand is strong and aircraft are unavailable, the airline risks missing revenue opportunities.

Restoring aircraft to service and securing additional capacity therefore becomes critical to the company’s financial strategy.

It also explains why delays involving spare parts and maintenance are so significant.

Every additional aircraft returned to operation potentially allows Kenya Airways to increase frequencies, protect schedules or deploy capacity where passenger demand is strongest.

Previous Financial Recovery Faces Another Test

The cost pressure comes after a turbulent financial period for Kenya Airways.

The airline recorded a rare pre-tax profit in 2024, marking a major milestone after years of financial difficulties.

That progress did not continue uninterrupted.

Kenya Airways subsequently reported a pre-tax loss of KSh17.93 billion for 2025, following lower revenues and operational difficulties.

The latest fuel shock means the airline must now control costs while simultaneously trying to improve fleet availability and maintain its network.

The contract review forms part of that effort.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Remains Part of Longer-Term Strategy

Despite immediate financial challenges, Kenya Airways continues pursuing longer-term sustainability initiatives.

In 2025, the airline operated an intra-African Nairobi–Cape Town flight using 50% Sustainable Aviation Fuel attributes under a mass-balance system.

Kenya Airways has also been working with Kenyan partners to develop domestic SAF capability and has identified locally sourced sustainable feedstocks as part of its longer-term strategy.

The carrier says its roadmap includes expanding SAF participation and supporting regional production.

These initiatives will not solve the immediate fuel-price problem. However, they demonstrate the airline’s attempt to address longer-term questions surrounding fuel sourcing, emissions and aviation sustainability.

Kenya Airways Situation Reflects Wider African Aviation Pressures

The problems facing Kenya Airways have implications beyond Kenya.

African carriers operate in an industry heavily dependent on international aircraft manufacturers, engine suppliers, maintenance networks and global energy markets.

Smaller fleets can make disruptions particularly difficult to manage.

If several aircraft become unavailable simultaneously, airlines have fewer replacements to protect schedules. Parts delays can then extend disruptions, while expensive fuel adds another layer of financial pressure.

This combination explains why fleet resilience and cost management have become increasingly important across African aviation.

Second Half of 2026 Becomes Critical for Kenya Airways

Kenya Airways now faces a demanding balancing act.

Passenger demand offers an important opportunity. Yet aircraft constraints limit the airline’s ability to fully exploit that demand, while the 72% fuel-cost increase places additional pressure on profitability.

Management’s decision to review contracts shows how seriously the carrier is approaching the cost challenge.

For passengers, there is currently no basis for assuming widespread route reductions or a general fare increase solely because of the fuel-cost announcement. Those would require separate decisions from the airline.

The bigger story is one of operational resilience.

Kenya Airways needs to secure aircraft, improve fleet availability, manage its supply chain and find savings without weakening the network that makes Nairobi one of Africa’s important aviation gateways.

text:
Insight Focus

SAF and SMF initiatives are gaining momentum globally. Canada and Brazil both advanced policies to support sustainable aviation fuel, while new projects and research highlighted the growing role of feedstocks such as corn, sugar and agricultural residues. As production expands, targeted SAF use could deliver outsized climate benefits, with just 2% of flights responsible for 80% of contrail-related warming.

With the need and desire to lower the carbon footprint of aviation and marine transportation, industry players, biofuel producers, and governments around the world are energetically driving the development of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and sustainable marine fuel (SMF) systems. These efforts are expected to create a major new market for ethanol produced from corn and sugar.

Canada Targets 10% SAF Use by 2030

A clear example came in August, when the Canadian government released a blueprint for the development of a sustainable aviation fuel industry in Canada. Transport Canada’s blueprint establishes a plan to meet the Aviation Climate Action Plan’s goal of 10% SAF use by 2030. Achieving that target would require an estimated 1 billion litres of SAF sourced from a combination of domestic production and international supply.

“Canada has the feedstock, refining expertise, innovation capacity and domestic airlines to create a world-leading industry that contributes to meeting its own needs and those of other jurisdictions,” Transport Canada stated in its blueprint.

Fred Ghatala, president of Advanced Biofuels Canada, welcomed the long-awaited government document. “The thing that the blueprint brings, and its most important contribution, is momentum. It signals Canadian government attention to this important issue,” he said.

Note: The maximum SAF production scenario is based on feedstock availability and expected technology readiness. The analysis suggests Canada’s domestic SAF production potential could reach up to 1.36 billion litres by 2030, with HEFA dominating near-term supply and PTL and GFT pathways becoming increasingly important by 2050. However, imports are still likely to be needed to meet long-term decarbonisation goals.

Source: Transport Canada

Brazil Signs SAF Mandate

Also in August, Brazil signed a decree regulating its National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program, or ProBioQAV, establishing the rules for the country’s SAF emissions reduction mandate and creating what the government says is the world’s first book-and-claim mechanism incorporated into public policy.

The ProBioQAV regulation establishes rules covering SAF production, certification, commercialisation and traceability, as well as compliance with greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for Brazil’s domestic aviation sector.

Australian SAF Project to Use Sugarcane Residue

Nextchem, through its subsidiary MyRechemical, has been awarded licensing, a process design package (PDP), and engineering services by SKY Renewables Burdekin, an Australian project development company focused on SAF production, for the syngas section of Project Lion in North Queensland’s Burdekin region.

The project will use locally available sugarcane residues as feedstock to produce purified, chemical-grade syngas through the application of NX Circular Gasification technology.

The syngas will then be used for subsequent conversion into SAF and renewable diesel through third-party solutions. Once at full operational scale, Project Lion has the potential to produce up to 125,000 tonnes of SAF per year.

By using sugarcane tops and trash, residual biomass that is often burned in the field, the project demonstrates how gasification enables the transformation of agricultural residues into an intermediate feedstock for low-carbon fuels, while supporting a more sustainable use of local biomass resources.

Sugarcane waste

Fabio Fritelli, managing director of Nextchem, said: “By leveraging our gasification technology, we can support the conversion of locally available sugarcane residues into low-carbon fuels, combining circular carbon solutions with the decarbonisation needs of aviation.”

SAF at Big Airports

An August report from the independent group Clean Air Task Force (CATF) found that directing SAF to a small number of high-impact airports, rather than spreading it across the aviation network, could significantly increase the fuel’s climate and public health benefits while global supply continues to build.

The report, Maximizing the Climate Co-Benefits of Sustainable Aviation Fuel via Targeted Allocation, analysed 2024 flight activity at major US and European airports to identify where targeted SAF use would have the greatest impact.

Working with aviation climate data company Estuaire, CATF analysed 16.6 million flights at major US and European airports in 2024, examining contrail formation as well as particulate matter and nitrogen oxide emissions during landing and take-off.

The analysis found that just 2% of flights generate 80% of contrail-related warming, meaning a targeted approach can capture most of the climate benefit without requiring a large share of the global SAF supply, which made up just 0.7% of the jet fuel market in 2025.
